Messages.Author: nys...@cs.com
Messages.Body:
I have not been a regular poster here for a while, so forgive if the
following issue has been discussed before. I am proposing a
tournament scoring system that seems to be an improvement over the
current one, and I am interested in feedback and counterarguments.

THE PROPOSED SYSTEM

Same as the current system, except:

1) No messing around with half victory points in uncompleted games.
A player gets a full victory point for not being ousted (whether due
to withdrawal or due to still being in the game when time is called).
This means that for uncompleted games, just like completed games, the
number of victory points distributed among the players equals the
number of players in the game.

2) For uncompleted games, 3 victory points (including the one for not
being ousted, if applicable) are required for a game win. For
completed games, one can still get a game win with 2 victory points
(on those very rare occasion when no-one else has 2 victory points).

WHY IT IS BETTER

1) It is more accurate in predicting what the outcome of the game is
likely to be if the game were played to completion (see, for instance,
the example below).

2) It is less encouraging of the sort of fast-vote and fast-bleed
decks that tend to dominate tournaments.

AN EXAMPLE

The following example seeks show why the proposed system is better
than the current system in predicting game outcomes:

In a five-player game, A (playing a fast, aggressive deck) ousts B &
C, then runs out of steam and gets ousted by E. D and E remain in the
game when it gets called for time.

Under the current system, players A, B, C, D and E get 2, 0, 0, .5 and
1.5 victory points respectively. A gets awarded a game win, E takes
second place.

This result, however, is dead wrong under the original rules. The one
thing we know for certain is that, under the original rules, it is
impossible for A to win the game. The best he can hope for is a tie
for first place (which is not a win).

If the game is played to a finish, there are only 3 ways it can end,
only 2 of which are even remotely likely, and NONE of which result in
a win for player A. Either E will oust D, in which case E will have 3
victory points and a game win, or else D will oust E, taking 2 victory
points, and tying with A so that nobody takes a game win. The third
possibility, withdrawal, results in 2 victory points for E (no matter
who withdraws) which is also a tie game with no winner.

If ANYONE in this called-for-time game should be granted a game win,
it should clearly be Player E, since he is the only person who has any
chance of winning it if it is played to a finish. Indeed, if we make
allowances for the fact that a person who starts winning is likely to
keep winning, his odds of emerging as winner may be greater than 50%.
Player A should not get it -- he is only the most successful of the
proven losers.

The proposed system has a fairer result. The five players get 2, 0,
0, 1, 2. Nobody gets a game win and Players A and E tie for first
place.

We cannot know whether D will end the game with 0 vp or 2 vp, so we
split the difference and give him 1 vp. We cannot know whether E will
end the game with 1 vp or 3 vp, so we split the difference and give
him 2.

ANTICIPATING SOME COUNTERARGUMENTS

1. "The point of the game is to oust people, not to sit there and
survive."

If the point of the game is really that simple, it is only because the
current tournament rules have made it so by devaluing survival. The
rule-book says differently. The rule-book says that survival or
withdrawal is worth as much as the ousting of a single prey. Of
course, the rulebook requires that one do more than merely survive in
order to win the game. In addition to survival, you will probably
need to oust two prey to win a completed 5-player game (in rare
situations, one prey ousted plus survival will suffice). So yes, you
need to do more than survive to win, just as you need to achieve more
than a single oust to win; but that does not mean that a single oust
should be worth more than survival.

Yes, the rules do require ousting, and should require ousting. The
proposed system reflects those values accurately.

2. "The current system encourages all players to play quickly in
order to maximize victory points for themselves as well as the whole
table; your proposed system might give a player currently in the lead,
or anyone in danger of being ousted, an incentive to stall."

This is true to some extent, but the force of this argument is very
much abated by the fact that game wins are the primary measure of
tournament success, with victory point totals being used only as tie
breakers. Under the proposed system, a game win is far more likely in
a finished game than an unfinished one, and I think this is all the
incentive for speed that is needed. If the game does not make
substantial progress, then nobody gets a game win.

And, although I agree that it would be better if games would finish, I
also feel that there can be too much of a good thing. An excessive
"hurry hurry hurry" atmosphere of tournament play does not necessarily
make for a relaxing and enjoyable tournament experience.

3. "Long drawn out games are boring, and are one of the flaws of
V:TES. It is good that tournament rules alter the game environment by
encouraging people to design decks that have some hope of proving
their worth within a 2 hour time limit."

Personally, I rather like long, drawn-out epic games. I am
nonetheless willing to assume, for the sake of argument, that long
games are bad for V:TES.

My response, again, is that the need to score a "game win" (rather
than merely survive or score more victory points than anyone else at
the table) is sufficient encouragement for people to design reasonably
fast decks intended to make substantial progress (including oustings)
within the 2-hour time limit.

And whatever the hostility toward drawn out games, I cannot help also
noting substantial hostility towards the sort of fast bleed/vote decks
that tend to do well in tournaments. People bemoan the fact that they
cannot bring to tournaments the "interesting" decks that they reserve
for casual play.

Seems to me that the system I propose is a suitable compromise,
offering reasonable encouragement to decks that can demonstrate SOME
progress within 2 hours, but not unfairly rewarding the fast weenie
deck that scores two victory points before it runs out of steam and
gets ousted.

I've already anticipated and responded to this argument -- but I'll
add another one. The argument simply proves too much. Not only does
it prove that a survivor should not get one victory point, but it also
proves that a survivor should not get a half victory point.

The question is not whether survivors should get credit, but how much
credit they should get. If you are not going to address that
question, then you have landed by accident in the wrong argument.

> If I'm in a game where I know I can't win, I can choose to wall up
> to the point that I'm now trying only to survive.

If you are really in a game where you "know you can't win" then you
can do this for a half victory point just as well as you can do it for
a whole victory point. Neither under the current system nor under the
proposed system is this strategy likely to be of much use in getting
you into the finals. Under either system, even a remote chance of a
game win is worth far more than any number of victory points without
such a win.

The single victory point you get for merely surviving is going to be
entirely worthless to you, especially if that is all your deck can
do. In a competitive environment, you need to do better than anyone
else, not merely keep the vp you brought to the table with you.

same effect? Are you objecting to my system, or to both systems. Do
you think that survivors should not even get the half point?

Messages.Body:
On Sep 24, 1:45 am, Bram Vink <jja.v...@hccnet.nl> wrote:
> On 24 sep, 07:51, nyst...@cs.com wrote:
> > Seems to me that the system I propose is a suitable compromise,
> > offering reasonable encouragement to decks that can demonstrate SOME
> > progress within 2 hours, but not unfairly rewarding the fast weenie
> > deck that scores two victory points before it runs out of steam and
> > gets ousted.
>
> Are those unfairly rewarded in the current system? Do you see many 2VP
> gamewins by such decks?

I claim no expertise regarding the tournament environment. My own
limited experience in my own local groups is that weenie fast bleed
and weenie fast vote are alot less common than they used to be. There
still seems to be a fair amount of player hostility towards those kind
of decks, however. It therefore seems strange that such decks would
be deliberately favored by a skewed tournament scoring system that
goes out of its way to reward fast decks, as opposed to a system that
more accurately reflects the original rules.

Nor would I be much concerned about the tournament environment, if not
for the effect it is having on my local group. My local group is
influenced by the tournament environment -- games are always called
after two hours, and any victory after the two-hour time limit is
openly disparraged as something that does not really count. Indeed,
games are often called after 1 hour and 45 minutes, on the ground that
not enough time remains for anyone to score the sort of victory that
might count in tournaments.

I have also noticed the effect on me, whenever I consider which of my
OWN decks I would consider playing in a tournament. For instance, I
do have one or two fast weenie bleed decks (such as a mono-obfuscate
bleed deck with burnable stealth). This deck has some chance of
sweeping, but when it fails at this aim, frequently fails by scoring
one or two victory points and then getting ousted.

I have other decks, which seem just as likely -- if not more likely --
to win a completed game, but face a serious question as to whether
they can do this within a 2-hour time limit. They might well win a 3-
hour final, if only it could make it into the finals. To my mind it
is just as good a deck -- if not a better deck -- but it will not make
the finals, in part because the tournament rules -- for no good reason
that I can think of -- devalue survival in games called for time.

But I do not claim my experience is typical -- my argument does not
depend on my expertise. My argument depends simply on the fact that
tournament scoring distorts and poorly estimates the outcome of
unfinished games. Does it matter how often a deck scores two victory
points and then gets ousted in a five player game that is then called
for time? Bottom line is, no matter what kind of deck this is,
whether weenie bleed or a fascinating and creative intercept combat
deck, that the tournament rules award such decks a game win that it
does not (under the standard rules) deserve. It awards a game win to
a player who we know for a fact could not have won the game had it
been completed.

> The thing concerning timeouts and such weenie decks is that they often
> do not happen simultaneously. I'd say there's an average of about 40
> turns playable in 2 hours (educated guess, but just that. These are
> turns all around the table) . If three people are ousted in the first
> 20 turns, that leaves 20 turns for 2 players to finish the game in.
> Perhaps a few more in a 1v1 endgame. But timeouts and super aggressive
> decks usually do not mix and match.

The point of what you are saying is lost on me. Are you suggesting
that it is impossible, or extremely unlikely, for a player to score
two victory points, then be ousted, and then have the game called for
time among the two remaining players? I assure you that that can and
does happen. And when it does happen, the tournament scoring system
awards the game win to the wrong person.

But this is only an extreme and striking example of the undervalueing
of surviving decks in games that get called for time. EVERY time a
game gets called for time (and this is NOT an uncommon occurrence),
the surviving players get a half victory point less than what what a
fair assessment of the strength of their position would award them.
This is a very serious consideration when choosing one's decks for
tournament play, and effectively prevents me from playing many
interesting decks I might otherwise want to try.

Suppose their are 5 players left when the game gets called for time.
We know only that, if the game is finished, Player A could get as many
as 5 victory points, or he may get none at all. A fair averaging of
the possibilities leaves him with the victory point he brought to the
table with him -- in short -- everyone should get a victory point.

There is no reason to impose a half-point penalty, unless we
deliberately want to punish those decks that win after 2 hours and
fifteen minutes, as opposed to those decks that win after one hour and
fifteen minutes.

Suppose their are two players left in a 4-player game, each with a
victory point. If the game is played to completion, one of these
players will get one victory point, whereas the other will get three.
A fair averaging of these possibilities gives them each 2 victory
points, not one and a half.

The judge of the tournament needs to choose the fifth player in a
tournament consisting of three rounds and a final. The next two
players in line each have one game win, so victory points will
determine the final round. Player A scored 3 vp in round one
(completed game); 1 victory points in round 2 (ousted in completed
game), and 1 victory point in round 3 (ousted in game called for time
after earning 1 vp) for a total of 5 vp. Player B, however, had the
misfortune to be stuck in slow games. He scored 2.5 vp in round one
(called for time with 2 players left); 1.5 vp in round 2 (called for
time with three players left); and 0.5 vp in round 3 (called for time
with 3 players left). He gets only 4.5 vp and therefore is knocked
out of the final running by player A. But a fair assessment of their
respective positions is that Player B is the stronger player. Had the
games been permitted to finish, the probabilities are very very
strongly in favor of his emerging with the most victory points. Even
without taking into account the fact that winning players tend to keep
winning, the law of averages suggest he would receive 6 victory
points, not 4.5.

Of course, it is possible that, had the games finished, he would have
received 3 vps; but it is also possible that, had the games finished,
he would have received 11 vps and 3 game wins. 6 vps fairly reflects
the law of averages and the strength of his position in the game.

There seems no compelling reason to impose this penalty. The fact
that his failure to finish rounds 2 and 3 has potentially deprived him
of one or two game wins is in itself an enormous penalty. Why impose
more beyond that? It just doesn't make sense

> So whereas I'm not yet commenting on the actual proposed rules, my
> question to you is, why would this change be neccessary? Is there a
> need for this?

I think I have adequately explained the need. I am now waiting for
someone to suggest some kind of justification for the half-point
penalty we currently impose on players remaining in a game that gets
called for time.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
<nys...@cs.com> wrote in message
news:1190657111....@57g2000hsv.googlegroups.com...

I claim no expertise regarding the tournament environment. My own
> limited experience in my own local groups is that weenie fast bleed
> and weenie fast vote are alot less common than they used to be. There
> still seems to be a fair amount of player hostility towards those kind
> of decks, however. It therefore seems strange that such decks would
> be deliberately favored by a skewed tournament scoring system that
> goes out of its way to reward fast decks, as opposed to a system that
> more accurately reflects the original rules.

Granted, fast weeny decks are always a problem in that they're hard things
for which to specifically build counter-decks. I mean, you _can_ build
counter decks for them, certainly, but not too many such decks are
otherwise viable in the greater metagame. So, acknowledging that, the
game also has (IMO) a distinct problem with decks which are too slow.
In this case, we're talking about fighty, intercepty combat decks which
stop up the whole table as they slowly build up and make it extremely
difficult for the anyone on the table to win except them - and they often
don't win either. Thus, the whole table gets punished for one deck's
"sins". Although your proposal would hurts them in a certain way (making
it difficult for them to get a game win if they don't finish the game)
and helps their opponents in a certain way (granting a whole VP for a
time-out), I think realistically it rewards them more (more whole victory
points for situations where they fail to win) and hurts their opponents
more (mainly their prey who feels little forward pressure from them may
get two VP but be unable to oust the intercepty deck) and so I wouldn't
think this was a positive proposal.

In general, the choice of the current GW criteria and withdrawal/time-out
rewards have been settled on from years of experience. They still strike
me as the best ones, absent more cogent reasons for changing them than
you've presented.

> I have also noticed the effect on me, whenever I consider which of my
> OWN decks I would consider playing in a tournament. For instance, I
> do have one or two fast weenie bleed decks (such as a mono-obfuscate
> bleed deck with burnable stealth). This deck has some chance of
> sweeping, but when it fails at this aim, frequently fails by scoring
> one or two victory points and then getting ousted.

This seems like a reason not to play them to me. So I'm confused what
your point is, here. I believe Darby Keeny played a weeny presence
bleed deck yesterday in the second day of the NAC. (Not absolutely sure
of the details since I didn't see him playing it but going from one of
his opponent's and his own description of it.) He got one table sweep
and nothing else (I believe) and failed to make the finals.

> There is no reason to impose a half-point penalty, unless we
> deliberately want to punish those decks that win after 2 hours and
> fifteen minutes, as opposed to those decks that win after one hour and
> fifteen minutes.

We deliberately want to punish those decks that win after 2 hours and

fifteen minutes, as opposed to those decks that win after one hour and

fifteen minutes, yes. The trouble with the former is that they make
it very difficult for OTHER decks to win at all. Thus, in a tournament
in which the time limit is two hours, you should be punished for bringing
a deck which has difficulty winning in less than two hours. Granted, the
penalty will also hit your opponents in that game - but since it's your
deck, you will get penalized all the time and your opponents will only
be penalized in the games they play with you. It's not a perfect answer
but it's the only one we really have.

> There seems no compelling reason to impose this penalty. The fact
> that his failure to finish rounds 2 and 3 has potentially deprived him
> of one or two game wins is in itself an enormous penalty. Why impose
> more beyond that? It just doesn't make sense

Why not? People REALLY shouldn't be bringing such decks. In fact, in
my observation people do bring slow decks sometimes and certain players
are good enough to win with them often enough that the payoff works for
them. But they should not be rewarded with a whole victory point for the
games which they fail to bring to a conclusion within the time limit.

Fred

> game win if they don't finish the game) [...]

I will respond to your other points later (it might take a while,
since I disagree with almost everything you say) but I want to get one
point out of the way, since it is an easy point.

You are mistaken about my current proposal making it harder for
intercept decks to score game wins. My current proposal makes it
almost exactly as hard for intercept decks to score a game win as the
current tournament rules do. To score a game win in an unfinished
game under my proposal, the intercept deck needs not merely to
survive, but also to score two ousts -- exactly as under the current
system.

The only way my proposal prevents intercept decks from gaining game
wins is by NOT giving a game win to an intercept deck that scores 2
vp's and then gets ousted. But this is not an outcome that is very
likely with intercept decks.

That's an interesting contention. Maybe I'm missing something - which
I certainly do from time to time - but could you please list what
the conditions are in which any kind of deck could get a GW under
your system where it wouldn't get one under the old system? I believe
the only ones would involve withdrawal, which is extremely difficult
to pull off absent player agreements. My experience is that withdrawals
in tournaments are extremely rare.

> The only way my proposal prevents intercept decks from gaining game
> wins is by NOT giving a game win to an intercept deck that scores 2
> vp's and then gets ousted.

OK, I see that I erred in claiming that it would make it harder for
them to get a game win in an unfinished game since if they had 1 and
1/2 VPs under the current system, they would have 2 VPs under your
proposal - not a GW in either case. And if they had 2 1/2 VPs under
the current system, they would get 3 VPs under your proposal which
is a GW in either system. Thus I stand corrected. None the less,
you likewise pointed out a way in which it would be harder for them
to get game wins under your proposal yet you hold that overall, it
helps intercept decks (whether by helping them get game wins is
disputed, apparently). Thus our positions are the same in this sense.
It's just that we differ whether there is any overall goodness to the
idea of helping or encouraging these sorts of decks in timed tournament.

Fred

I am not sure I understand why you are asking the question. Did I
ever say anything to imply that my proposed system would EVER have
such an effect?

It does make slower decks (but not the slowest decks) marginally more
competitive -- but not by granting them game wins. One (very
marginal) way it help them is to prevent faster competition from being
awarded game wins in games where they certainly would not have won a
completed game. A more substantive benefit is the advantage in
victory points, but the effect is not earth shattering since this is
only used as a tie-breaker for game wins.

Of course, if a slower deck makes it into the 3-hour final, as a
result of the above advantages, it may end up winning the tournament
(taking full advantage of the extra time to prove its worth), which is
a game win it would not have otherwise achieved.

It is a cautious and modest proposal, neither intended nor likely to
have any radical effect on the game environment.

> to pull off absent player agreements. My experience is that withdrawals
> in tournaments are extremely rare.

I agree -- which perhaps explains why I did not bother mentioning it.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
On Sep 24, 1:51 am, nyst...@cs.com wrote:
> 1) No messing around with half victory points in uncompleted games.
> A player gets a full victory point for not being ousted (whether due
> to withdrawal or due to still being in the game when time is called).
> This means that for uncompleted games, just like completed games, the
> number of victory points distributed among the players equals the
> number of players in the game.

Hmm. You may have missed all the brujaja in recent months, but there
is a lot of concern over games timing out by design (more or less),
and givine even greater incentive to time out (i.e. getting 1VP for
timing out instead of .5) makes timing out even more attractive--if
simply surviving is as good as ousting your prey, in situations where
you think you can only oust your one prey but it is risky, it becomes
more beneficial simply to wall up and survive, rather than taking the
risky option to try and oust your prey.

Anything that removes incentive to oust your prey is Bad.

> 2) It is less encouraging of the sort of fast-vote and fast-bleed
> decks that tend to dominate tournaments.

Why? Fast decks will still oust and get VPs, as fast decks don't
benefit from slwing the game down. They benefit from ousting their
prey.

> If the point of the game is really that simple, it is only because the
> current tournament rules have made it so by devaluing survival.

The game is about ousting your prey.

> The
> rule-book says differently. The rule-book says that survival or
> withdrawal is worth as much as the ousting of a single prey.

A) Withdrawing from the game is generally considerably harder than
simply surviving till the game runs out of time.

B) The tournament rules currently stipulate you only get .5 VP for
withdrawing anyway. To remove the incentive to use withdrawl as a
dealmaking tool. To encourage folks to oust their prey.

> Yes, the rules do require ousting, and should require ousting. The
> proposed system reflects those values accurately.

Yet gives more incentive to not try and oust your prey if it seems
risky to do so and gives more incentive to try and just wall up and
make the game time out if you are in a bad position.

If you get .5 VP for surviving and 1 VP for ousting your prey,
however, there is *always* concrete incentive to try and go forward.
Even if it is risky. As the reward for the risk outweighs the reward
for inaction.

> And whatever the hostility toward drawn out games, I cannot help also
> noting substantial hostility towards the sort of fast bleed/vote decks
> that tend to do well in tournaments. People bemoan the fact that they
> cannot bring to tournaments the "interesting" decks that they reserve
> for casual play.

I, for one, would much rather see games that have fast decks and
result in people getting ousted than not.

-Peter

> On Sep 24, 7:22 pm, "Frederick Scott" <nos...@no.spam.dot.com> wrote:
>> Maybe I'm missing something - which
>> I certainly do from time to time - but could you please list what
>> the conditions are in which any kind of deck could get a GW under
>> your system where it wouldn't get one under the old system?
>
> I am not sure I understand why you are asking the question. Did I
> ever say anything to imply that my proposed system would EVER have
> such an effect?

Sort of, yea. If it's exactly as hard to get a GW and you can no longer
get one after gaining two VP and being ousted, there must be another
situation somewhere else to make up for that. But never mind, in
truth it's mostly that I misread what you were claiming in your
previous post. I note that it's also harder for others to get game wins
by ousting two players and then being ousted when a game times out -
since the opponent who ousted them will now have two VP and tie them
whereas before the latter would only have 1 and 1/2 VP. (And the time-
out goal of 3 VP would be in effect - something the ousted player no
longer has any power over despite it affecting him.) So that's
another kind of 'reward' (i.e. preventing an opponent from getting a
GW) for a deck that didn't show enough offense to resolve the game in
two hours. Bad.

> It is a cautious and modest proposal, neither intended nor likely to
> have any radical effect on the game environment.

Perhaps not - except in its tendency to cause more tied (and thus
unawarded) game wins. But it just rewards exactly the wrong style of
play, IMHO.

Fred

Messages.Author: nys...@cs.com
Messages.Body:
On Sep 25, 12:50 pm, "Frederick Scott" <nos...@no.spam.dot.com> wrote:
> I note that it's also harder for others to get game wins
> by ousting two players and then being ousted when a game times out -
> since the opponent who ousted them will now have two VP and tie them
> whereas before the latter would only have 1 and 1/2 VP.

Right. This was the example I chose for my original post.

> (And the time-
> out goal of 3 VP would be in effect - something the ousted player no
> longer has any power over despite it affecting him.)

I'm not sure what you mean, but I suspect you are making a mistake.
You seem to be accusing my proposal of a flaw of which it is quite
innocent, but which the current system is actually guilty.

Only in extremely rare situtations can you score a game win with 2
victory points in a completed 4 or 5-player game. One of these rare
situations involves withdrawals by multiple players, and is not even
worth discussing. In the other, E gets ousted by D, who in turn gets
ousted by C, who in turn gets ousted by B, who in turn gets ousted by
A, permitting a situation where A, B, C, D, and E get 2, 1, 1, 1 and 0
vps respectively. What makes this situation so ridiculously unlikely
is that it always requires the last person to score a vp to be the
next person ousted, despite the fact that ousting normally strengthens
a player by earning them pool. In short, a 2 vp victory is merely a
theoretical possiblity that no-one should expect. The normal
requirement for victory in a 4 or 5 player game is 3 vp.

Being ousted normally means a non-win. In a 5-player game, a person
who finally gets ousted by the last player after ousting everyone else
is the winner with 3 vps, but this is the only exception that exists
in games with fewer than six players. There are NO situations where,
in a completed game, an ousted person with 2 victory points can win.

When person scores two victory points and then gets ousted, the
theoretical possibility of a 2vp victory is no longer a possiblity --
this game will be won by someone gaining 3 vps, or it will not be won
at all. Depending on what happens next, he will either tie with a
player for 2 vp, or lose to a player with 3 victory points. He will
not win. Period.

Under my proposed system, he is not granted a game win merely because
the last two people standing fail to finish the game. He is NOT
affected by what they do after he is ousted.

Under the current system, he WILL be granted a game win if the last
two players are called for time, and WON'T be granted a game win if
they manage to finish the game. So it is the CURRENT system that
punishes or rewards him based on what happens after he is ousted.

In fact (and I only just thought of this) this scenario could give one
of the last two players an incentive to throw the game to his
opponent, in order to deprive Player A (who scored 2 vps and then got
ousted) or a game win. If this scenario, one of the last 2 players
(player E) has 1 vp, and the other (Player D) has 0 vp. If the game
goes to time, A will win with 2, 0, 0, 1.5, 0.5. But if player E lets
himself be ousted D, then he will prevent A from getting a game win at
a cost of a half-victory point. This creates a final score of 2, 0,
0, 1, 2 -- and nobody gets a game win. Player E might consider this a
perfecely reasonable option if, in the last 5 minutes of the game, he
realizes he cannot oust his opponent and get the game win himself.
Despite the cost of a half vp, depriving an opponent of a game win
could maximize Player E's chances of making it into the finals.

My proposed system avoids such silliness.

I still have to respond to your other points. Forgive me if I take my
time. Writing is exhausting for me, and I seem to be quite
outnumbered here.

<nys...@cs.com> wrote in message

> On Sep 25, 12:50 pm, "Frederick Scott" <nos...@no.spam.dot.com> wrote:
>> I note that it's also harder for others to get game wins
>> by ousting two players and then being ousted when a game times out -

>> whereas before the latter would only have 1 and 1/2 VP.
>
> Right. This was the example I chose for my original post.

...and another thing that I would deem a negative, since the ousted
player (one would assume) took risks to resolve the game sooner (a
good thing in my value system) whereas the player who (one would
assume) had the upper hand at the end of the game failed to move
aggressively enough to resolve it (a bad thing in my value system).
I strongly prefer the former get a game win and the latter be
penalized.

>> (And the time-
>> out goal of 3 VP would be in effect - something the ousted player no
>> longer has any power over despite it affecting him.)
>
> I'm not sure what you mean, but I suspect you are making a mistake.
> You seem to be accusing my proposal of a flaw of which it is quite
> innocent, but which the current system is actually guilty.
>

> victory points in a completed 4 or 5-player game. One of these rare
> situations involves withdrawals by multiple players, and is not even
> worth discussing. In the other, E gets ousted by D, who in turn gets
> ousted by C, who in turn gets ousted by B, who in turn gets ousted by
> A, permitting a situation where A, B, C, D, and E get 2, 1, 1, 1 and 0
> vps respectively. What makes this situation so ridiculously unlikely
> is that it always requires the last person to score a vp to be the
> next person ousted, despite the fact that ousting normally strengthens
> a player by earning them pool. In short, a 2 vp victory is merely a
> theoretical possiblity that no-one should expect. The normal
> requirement for victory in a 4 or 5 player game is 3 vp.

(Just as an aside...)
Well, actually this is the archetypical "back-oust" and is not all that
rare. Certain kinds of decks are constructed to back-oust (but aren't
considered mainstream, of course, because so many things can go wrong)
and sometimes rush decks do it more or less by accident (either by
encountering successive predators who can only be neutralized through
their utter destruction or by accidentally destroying them). Granted,
it's not a common occurrence but it happens - especially in four-
player games.

> Being ousted normally means a non-win.

It depends on what you mean. Under the current system, two VPs before
oust can be a game win, if the remaining players are ineffective in
ousting one another before time. I believe that's how if should be.
Your change would eliminate that feature. My parenthetical comment
you wished to respond to above was just to point out that the standard
for a game win hinges on whether the game was completed or not and the
ousted player has no control over that. Nothing more. If your reply
is just that under your proposed system it doesn't matter (since he isn't
going to get a game win either way), OK - so noted. It wasn't really
important anyway which was why I used the parenthesis.

> In fact (and I only just thought of this) this scenario could give one
> of the last two players an incentive to throw the game to his
> opponent, in order to deprive Player A (who scored 2 vps and then got
> ousted) or a game win. If this scenario, one of the last 2 players
> (player E) has 1 vp, and the other (Player D) has 0 vp. If the game
> goes to time, A will win with 2, 0, 0, 1.5, 0.5. But if player E lets
> himself be ousted D, then he will prevent A from getting a game win at
> a cost of a half-victory point. This creates a final score of 2, 0,
> 0, 1, 2 -- and nobody gets a game win. Player E might consider this a
> perfecely reasonable option if, in the last 5 minutes of the game, he
> realizes he cannot oust his opponent and get the game win himself.
> Despite the cost of a half vp, depriving an opponent of a game win
> could maximize Player E's chances of making it into the finals.

Sure. But, in practice, it seldom does. And, for what it's worth, that
kind of reasoning is illegal because it doesn't pass muster under the
play-to-win rule. Tournament standing is considered an "out-of-game
motivation". In practice, this is difficult to enforce because in many
instances the judge would have to read player E's mind to have any
evidence that an illegal play happened. But at the very least, it
prevents the remaining players from speaking of this and making
out-loud deals around it.

> My proposed system avoids such silliness.

It isn't really considered a problem, as far as I know. If a player is
on the bubble, the 1/2 victory point makes the difference between him
and anyone else he's tied with for game wins and victory points or could
become tied with (thus leaving it to tournament points and/or
randomization). Preventing player A from gaining a game win only helps
him against player A. If he has knowledge that player A is the only
player he needs to compete with for that last spot in the finals and
that preventing player A from getting a game win is the only way to do
it, this might make a difference. But in a tournament with eight or more
players, that is almost never the case and when it is, player E will
seldom be aware of it. Trust me, this is a miniscule thing.

> I still have to respond to your other points. Forgive me if I take my
> time. Writing is exhausting for me, and I seem to be quite
> outnumbered here.

Well, the obvious issue is the original one cited: why reward decks that
are so slow and deliberate that they excessively risk going to time and
preventing all players from getting a game win? If we have any other
real issues beyond that, I fail to see what they could be.

Fred

Messages.Author: nys...@cs.com
Messages.Body:
Peter D Bakija wrote:
> On Sep 24, 1:51 am, nyst...@cs.com wrote:>
> > 1) No messing around with half victory points in uncompleted
> > games. A player gets a full victory point for not being ousted
> > (whether due to withdrawal or due to still being in the game when
> > time is called). This means that for uncompleted games, just like
> > completed games, the number of victory points distributed among
> > the players equals the number of players in the game.
>
> Hmm. You may have missed all the brujaja in recent months, but
> there is a lot of concern over games timing out by design (more or

> less), [...]

I did a bit of searching, and all I could find recently was some posts
about FINALISTS who seem willing to permit the final round to go to
time because they don't need a "game win" to win the tournament. But
this can hardly be what you had in mind. As I am sure you realize --
my proposed system has no affect on such dynamics whatsoever, for
better or worse.

Since you said "by design" I guess you are talking about players
deliberately orchestrating "time outs", and not merely talking about
issues of game design and game mechanics that make survival too easy
and ousting too hard. If the problem is merely one of game design &
game mechanics, resulting in games running too long (whatever you
think "too long" is), then the solution, in my opinion, is for the
design team to print new cards that tend to promote faster games. I'm
sure the design team has been doing just that -- and/or will do just
that -- to the extent that they perceive a problem.

Unless you want to actually ban blood dolls and bleed defense (and
such), then printing new cards that promote fast games seems to me the
ONLY solution to any alleged problem. Such a solution does NOT involve
blaming the players when their games go to time, nor should it.
Virtually all players are doing the best they can to win the game --
which is exactly what they should be doing.

Until you elaborate, I will presume you are discussing the same
phenomenon I have noticed. The problem I have noticed is players
getting understandably frustrated when games go to time because a time
out HURTS THEM by depriving them -- not only of their hopes of of
victory -- but also of the reasonable value of their reasonable
expectations. To use the simplest example: If 2 players are left in
a game, it is reasonable to suppose that, if the game is permitted to
continue indefinitely, one will eventually oust the other. In other
words, each has about 50-50 chance of winning 2 victory points (above
and beyond whatever they may have already earned). As any gambler or
mathematician knows, a 50-50 chance of 2 vp is worth one vp, not half
a vp.

A more negative aspect of this phenomenon of understandable player
frustration is the phenomenon of mean-spirited, petulant and
unsportsmanlike players, unhappy at the game outcome, taking out their
otherwise-understandable frustration at what they call "Bad Players"
who kept everyone else (and especially a Certain Someone) from gaining
victory points, without scoring any victory points themselves. I
seriously hope that whiny losers of this variety have not been getting
a sympathetic ear on this NG. To my mind, petulant tantrume directed
at one's fellow losers is even more reprehensible than petulance at
the winner. At least the winner knows he won and can laugh in your
face. But the fellow loser often knows that (to some extent) he did
play badly -- that's why he lost, and the whiny loser may succeed in
making him feel bad. But it the whiny loser were honest with himself,
he would acknowledge that he does not really want his opponent to play
better -- he wants them to play worse.

My solution to this problem (both the understandable frustration and
the unsportsmanlike petulance) would be to reduce player frustration
by granting players the fair victory-point value of their position in
the game when it times out.

This will not (as a general rule) make them WANT games to time out,
because, under my system, one still needs to score two ousts for a
game win. The only people (apart from tournament finalists discussed
above) likely to WANT to "merely" surive til time out under my
proposed system are people who have already scored two ousts and are
therefore guaranteed a game win provided no-one ousts them (and it is
hardly fair to call that "merely" surviving til time out). But this
is not a flaw compared to the current system, because the current
system works almost exactly the same way in this regard.

> [...] and giving even greater incentive to time out (i.e. getting 1VP

> for timing out instead of .5) makes timing out even more attractive--

This, to me, seems somewhat analogous to saying that letting drivers
wear seatbelts while driving makes crashing their car more
attractive. It may be, in some very marginal sense, true that if we
don't let drivers wear seatbelts they might drive a tiny bit more
carefully, but on the whole it is a poor argument against seatbelts.

My proposed system is not going to make players any more eager for 5-
way tie games than current drivers are eager to crash their cars. I
expect players will still try to win the game in much the same that
seatbelted drivers will still try to avoid crashing into other
vehicles. They just might be a little less unhappy when they fail,
since they will not be unfairly treated compared.

> [...] if simply surviving is as good as ousting your prey, in

> situations where you think you can only oust your one prey but it
> is risky, it becomes more beneficial simply to wall up and survive,
> rather than taking the risky option to try and oust your prey.

First of all, a single oust IS worth the same as survival. The rules
(which are applied more or less intact in completed games even in
tournaments) say so. If you don't like that, you can advocate that
the rules be changed. It would certainly be possible to have a game
where only ousts were counted as victory points. In such a game, one
who scored 2 ousts in a 4-player game would win, even if the final
player then ousted him.

This would also create a situation where granting a half vp for
survival in uncompleted games would (for 2 surviving players) more or
less fairly reflect the strength of their position in the game (the
one remaining vp is divided equally between them).

Under the current rules, however, the above situation is a tie game,
despite the fact that the surviving player has only one oust, wheras
his opponent has two ousts.

An oust is worth the same as ultimate survival. However, you
generally need 3 vps for a game win, and you can only survive once, so
ousts are (collectively) more important than being the last player
standing.

It hardly follows, however, that players will roll over and let
themselves be ousted if we give them the right incentive. An ousted
methuselah can do nothing. Not only has he no chance whatsoever of
ousting his prey, but he cannot even have fun playing his cards and
learning what it is about his deck that works and what does not.

> Anything that removes incentive to oust your prey is Bad.

Irrelevant, since my proposed system does not remove the incentive to
oust your prey. Two ousts are still required for a game win (ignoring
rare exceptions).

But if you mean something more than that, you have said too much. You
cannot really mean that anything which has any potential whatsoever to
prolong a game is bad.

If you really mean what you say, perhaps you think the game would be
even better if the players received NO points for surviving in timed
out games. Then they would be in even more of a panic to finish;
would take greater risks. They might even deliberately oust
themselves (after a coin flip) to let the game finish (doesn't cost
them anything).

We could try as an experiment a game where we simply raced to see who
could be the first to score an oust. That person would be declared
the winner, period! But if, after trying such an experiment, you
found you were dissatisfied, and wanted to return to the old way, an
opponent could counter with "anything that removes your incentive to
oust your prey is bad."

> > 2) It is less encouraging of the sort of fast-vote and fast-bleed
> > decks that tend to dominate tournaments.
>
> Why?

For the reasons I stated. No need to repeat myself since I am sure
you understood me.

> Fast decks will still oust and get VPs, [...]

Indeed. My proposal is neither intended nor likely to have any
radical effects.

> > If the point of the game is really that simple, it is only
> > because the current tournament rules have made it so by
> > devaluing survival.
>
> The game is about ousting your prey.

Please stop pretending you didn't understand me. Please stop
pretending I am trying to eliminate the need for ousting. I am
perfectly aware that ousting is required, and should be required, for
victory, and you are arguing with a straw man if you try to pretend
otherwise.

However, under the current rules for completed games, the number of
ousts is not the only factor used to determine victory. If you think
it SHOULD be the only factor, then say so, but don't pretend that is
how it IS.

A person who scores a single oust, and then gets ousted, gets one
victory point. A person who merely avoids getting ousted, and
survives until the last person in the game withdraws, gets one victory
point.

Neither are winners, because 3 vps are generally needed for victory in
a 4-5 player game. But the "mere" single-ouster is not rated higher
than the "mere" survivor.

If you think it should be otherwise, then we need to change the rules.

> > The
> > rule-book says differently. The rule-book says that survival or
> > withdrawal is worth as much as the ousting of a single prey.
>
> A) Withdrawing from the game is generally considerably harder than
> simply surviving till the game runs out of time.

I'm not sure why you are telling me this. I only mentioned withdrawal
for completeness, to avoid the annoyance of someone coming correcting
me.

> B) The tournament rules currently stipulate you only get .5 VP for
> withdrawing anyway. To remove the incentive to use withdrawl as a
> dealmaking tool. To encourage folks to oust their prey.

I don't think it was primarily "To encourage folks to oust their
prey." I think it was understood that the players already had that
incentive, and only resorted to the withdrawal device when they
realized that their hopes and efforts had failed.

I just think it was felt that, if one of several players cannot
overcome the others, he should not gain more victory points in the
final round by agreeing to a draw by one method rather than by
another. It is simply an abuse of the withdrawal rule to use it for
such purposes. It takes advantage of the tension between the rules
for completed games and the rules for uncompleted games. A 5-way draw
is a 5-way draw is a 5-way draw. A deadlock is a deadlock is a
deadlock. Why should a 5-way draw at one table give its players more
points than a 5-way draw at another table? If you have not, in any
way, bested your opponents, why should you gain extra credit?

But such problems still potentially exist under the current rules.
Imagine 5 players left at the table. Each player has 5 or more
minions, but 5 or less pool. With 15 seconds to go, Player A calls
Ancilla Empowerment. Everyone with votes sees the implications and
votes in favor. Everyone gets ousted simultaneously, and everyone
gets a victory point. Meanwhile, a similarly deadlocked game at a
nearby table goes to time, and everyone there gets a half victory
point.

The second situation is an abuse for the same reason that the first
situation is an abuse. It gives the players extra credit despite the
fact that no player at the table got the better of any other person at
the table.

Note that the problem, in the second situation, is not that the player
was not interested in ousting his prey. If anything, he was too
interested in ousting his prey. He ousted his prey under
circumstances where ousting bore no relationship whatsoever to winning
or besting his opponents.

Victory points should be awarded based on one's success in besting
other players at your table. You should not be competing with other
tables, by trying to maximize the total number of victory points
distributed at your table compared to other tables. The number of
vp's handed out at a table should always be the same -- 1 vp per
player -- regardless of whether the game gets called for time.

My proposal eliminates both abuses (without skewing the results for
completed games where withdrawal occurs).

> > Yes, the rules do require ousting, and should require ousting.
> > The proposed system reflects those values accurately.
>
> Yet gives more incentive to not try and oust your prey if it seems
> risky to do so and gives more incentive to try and just wall up and
> make the game time out if you are in a bad position.

I'm sorry, but that's pretty much what one SHOULD do if one is in a
bad position. Nobody has an obligation to give up and let themselves
be ousted just because they realize they cannot score a game win. I
see no evidence that anyone is walling up under any other
circumstances, nor am I inclined to second guess the judgment of other
players.

Of course, one can and does take risks in Jyhad, in the hope of
victory. But, for reasons explained below, this does not depend very
much on the price tag you place on survival.

> If you get .5 VP for surviving and 1 VP for ousting your prey,
> however, there is *always* concrete incentive to try and go
> forward. Even if it is risky. As the reward for the risk outweighs
> the reward for inaction.

I understand what you are saying. It is sort of a gambler's
argument. Suppose Player A says to himself -- "If I tap out all my
minions, I have a 40 percent chance of earning a dollar, but on the
downside, their is also an independent 50 percent chance that I will
lose a dollar. On the average, I can expect to lose 10 cents on this
deal, I won't do it." But if you reduce the potential loss to 50
cents, then the equation is (.40 times 1,00 is .40) minus (.50 time .
50 is .25) equals a situation where on average the gambler can earn 15
cents, and therefore thinks it a good deal to go forward.

The problem is that, in jyhad, a player the point is not to count
pennies. The point is to win the game, by beating your opponents, and
not letting them beat you.

A player who gets ousted does not lose 50 cents; he does not lose a
dollar. He loses the game, and gets kicked out of the game. I know
there are rare exceptions. In a 5 player game, for instance, a player
who scores 3 ousts is a victor even if he then gets ousted. But to
achieve this he had to survive at least long enough to score three
ousts -- in fact, despite the fact that he was the last player
standing, he had to survive until the very end of the game.

A player who lets himself be one of the first 2 or 3 players ousted in
a game has failed. He has failed regardless of any silly attempts to
place a discounted value on his survival. He has no chance of earning
any future victory points. He does not even have the reward of being
able to have fun playing around with his cards so he can learn how to
make his deck better.

He came to win (something he generally cannot do without surviving til
the end of the game), and, failing that, he came to score an oust or
two (something he cannot do without surviving a substantial part of
the game), and failing that, he came to get that lousy half vp he gets
for surviving under the current system, and, failing that, he came to
hold out as long as possible before being ousted so he could spend as
much time as possible playing cards and having fun and as little time
as possible sitting on the sidelines feeling bored. You really think
he will feel happier about being ousted if you tell him that his
survival was only worth a half victory point instead of one? Do you
suppose he would play much differently if you reduced the survival
award to zero?

The need for a game win already means that there is concrete incentive
to try to oust, regardless of whether survival is discounted in time-
out games.

> > And whatever the hostility toward drawn out games, I cannot help
> > also noting substantial hostility towards the sort of fast
> > bleed/vote decks that tend to do well in tournaments. People
> > bemoan the fact that they cannot bring to tournaments the
> > "interesting" decks that they reserve for casual play.
>
> I, for one, would much rather see games that have fast decks and
> result in people getting ousted than not.

Of course, there is some circularity here. Part of the reason you
want to see fast games is because you want to avoid the time out
penalty, a problem I am proposing we correct.

But, even if you do just prefer fast games, that does not help much.
I'm not sure what your definition of a "fast deck" is. Other players
have their own preferences, and obviously the solution cannot be to
have you tell them what sort of decks they may or may not bring to
the tournament. You're not supposed to know what I'm bringing, and
I'm not supposed to know what you're bringing.

Many of the factors that cause games to go to time are beyond player
control. Each player is trying to win, and there are 4 other players
at the table trying to stop him. The only way players can truly
control the situation is to let themselves be ousted, which they
should not do. Generally, all players, whatever their errors in
judgment, are playing to the best of their ability. Each tries to
outguess the other. A player whose deck has too little offense, or
the wrong kind of offense, together with too much defense, or the
right kind of defense, has merely made an error in guessing his
opposition. And if he decides to wall up and survive, he is virtually
always making the best of a bad situation, to the best of his limited
judgment.

> I strongly prefer the former get a game win and the latter be
> penalized.

Why are you making assumpions not inherent in the fact pattern?

The only "value systems" I am aware of are the current tournament
rules for scoring incomplete games, which declare the above player a
winner, and the standard rules for scoring complete games, which
declare him a loser. Player A played well under the former value
system, and badly under the latter. Why should there be this tension
between the two value systems, when Player A has no control over what
happens after he is ousted? Would it not be better for Player A to
know which "value system" will judge him while he still has a chance
to do something about it?

If you really think that Player A needs to be rewarded with victory,
after scoring 2 vps and then being ousted, then perhaps we should
change the standard rules. If we deprive players of the extra 1 vp
they get for being the last player standing, then our ousted player
has a reasonable chance of winning even if the game is completed. The
worst he can do is tie. There will be less tension between the
completed game and the incomplete game.

If you want to make absolute sure he keeps his well-deserved reward,
we could further introduce a rule that the winner is the first person
to gain 2 vp, regardless of whether another player gains 2 vp later in
the game (simultaneous vps are still a tie).

But somehow, the "value system" of the original rules seems more
appealing to me. It avoids the strange situation of an ousted
"winner" sitting bored on the sidelines as he waits for the game to
finish, watching the happy losers as having fun as they jockey for
second place (and, unless you choose both of the above rules changes,
waiting helplessly to see if his crown will be taken from him).

Under the current rules (for completed games), the only situations I
can think of where an ousted player can win is where the game ends
immediately after he is ousted.

It's a minor point, yes, but still (I think) worth mentioning.

The standard rulebook rules, for completed 4 or 5-player games, do not
allow for a situation where an ousted player sits around watching the
game waiting to see if he has won or not.

situation, granting the ousted player a game win only if the remaining

from a continuing game is never a game winner, regardless of whether
the game later goes to time. Hence my proposal is more consistent
with the rules for finished games.

would guess that someone decided it was unfair that a person who went
to time with a single vp should earn the exact same result.

Of course, now that game wins are treated as a primary determination,
that is no longer the issue.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
In article <1191117326....@19g2000hsx.googlegroups.com>,
nys...@cs.com wrote:

> I did a bit of searching, and all I could find recently was some posts
> about FINALISTS who seem willing to permit the final round to go to
> time because they don't need a "game win" to win the tournament. But
> this can hardly be what you had in mind.

Why can that hardly be what I had in mind? There has been an awful lot
of discussion of late specifically about final games going to time and
not actually ending with a concrete winner--instead the winner being
determined by tiebreakers (i.e. the final ends with 3 people left at the
table, 2 of them each have 1VP, the guy with the higher initial seed
wins! Woo!)

> As I am sure you realize --
> my proposed system has no affect on such dynamics whatsoever, for
> better or worse.

Your proposed system gives 1VP for survival. This encourages folks to
try a lot harder to not die as opposed to oust their prey, which has an
effect on the whole dynamic.

> Until you elaborate, I will presume you are discussing the same
> phenomenon I have noticed. The problem I have noticed is players
> getting understandably frustrated when games go to time because a time
> out HURTS THEM by depriving them -- not only of their hopes of of
> victory -- but also of the reasonable value of their reasonable
> expectations.

Games going to time hurts folks 'cause no one actually wins the game. If
folks want someone to win the game, they should try harder to oust their
prey. Giving folks more incentive to wall up and *not* try and oust
their prey, isn't going to improve this dynamic.

> First of all, a single oust IS worth the same as survival. The rules
> (which are applied more or less intact in completed games even in
> tournaments) say so. If you don't like that, you can advocate that
> the rules be changed.

I don't need to advocate that the rules be changed--as the rules stand,
you get .5VP for surviving. If you are the last person at the table, you
get a full VP for survival, as being the last guy at the table is a
considerably more significant event that simply surviving till time runs
out. Which is why you get 1VP for being last guy at the table and only
.5VP for not being ousted when time runs out.

> Irrelevant, since my proposed system does not remove the incentive to
> oust your prey. Two ousts are still required for a game win (ignoring
> rare exceptions).

Giving 1VP for still being at the table when time runs out removes
incentive to oust your prey in any remotely risky situation, as defense
(i.e. walling up and covering your head) is generally less risky than
offense (going all out to oust your prey even if it means you might fail
and get ousted). If the reward in a difficult situation is 1VP for
walling up and covering your head instead of .5VP, you have incentive to
wall up and cover your head rather than lunging for the risky oust.
Anything that disincentives folks going for the risky oust is bad.

> If you really mean what you say, perhaps you think the game would be
> even better if the players received NO points for surviving in timed
> out games.

I'd be ok with that. Except that, as you note, it makes folks arbitrary
and reckless. Which is why the current system is reasonable--you have
more incentive to try and go forward than to simply survive, but more
incentive to survive than to get ousted.

> Please stop pretending you didn't understand me. Please stop
> pretending I am trying to eliminate the need for ousting.

It is called "rhetorical device", not "pretending".

> Victory points should be awarded based on one's success in besting
> other players at your table.

Sure. Simply staying alive is not success in besting other players at
the table. Which is why you get .5VP for still being alive when time
runs out, rather than 1VP. As more often than not, being alive when time
runs out has nothing at all to do with ones actual in game position--you
could easily be at 1 pool, next to go, and sitting in front of an Anarch
Revolt without the Edge when time runs out during your predator's turn.
You survive, sure, but only by arbitrary time limit, not by virtue of
game play. Consequently, the general consensus is that .5VP for
survivial at time is a reasonable compromise.

> I'm sorry, but that's pretty much what one SHOULD do if one is in a
> bad position.

See, clearly you do think this, as your proposal encourages this. Which
I don't believe is actually a good idea. To reward folks for not trying
to oust their prey. The tournament rules need to reward folks for trying
to oust their prey over simply surviving. Giving .5VP for surviving is a
reasonable compromise.

ultimately what should be optimized.

I think it's better that a player who got two VP and then ousted be
granted a GW if no remaining player got more than one VP in a timed
out game. Period. I think this because the relative valuation of
outcomes between the player who ousted two other players at the risk
of his own ability to remain in the game is higher than the remaining
player(s) who could not oust more than one other player even though
they survived the game. Such a comparison obviously doesn't hold if
the game is completed, so tinkering with the current system in the
way you propose wouldn't yield anything positive.

> Under the current rules (for completed games), the only situations I
> can think of where an ousted player can win is where the game ends
> immediately after he is ousted.

I'm not sure what you mean by this. Under the current rules, I believe
the only situation where an ousted player can win a completed game would
involve withdrawals by at least one other player.

It does do that by removing the 1/2 point penalty for being in a

They are lower on the heirarchy of determiners but they come into
play quite often so their contribution should not be understated.

> My proposal marginally
> rewards successful decks by providing a fairer approximation of the
> ultimate game outcome.

Your definition of "successful decks" is a stab at a circular
argument: by defining these particular decks as a "successful", you
infer it would be a good thing that they should be rewarded. I
reject the definition.

Again, what seems to be at issue here is your insistence on
approximating successful behavior in non-timed games with tournament
scoring that matches it. This is not important to me. See the
last paragraph of the post where I responded to my own post.

> me I ought not play it. I said I had some slower decks, and you said
> I ought not play them either. I am forced to conclude that, in your

If your decks can't win within the time limit of the tournament, you
can and should be penalized for that, yes. Again, such behavior robs
other players of their chance to get game wins within the time limit
and that's bad. As for being "welcome" or not, you're always welcome
to join a tournament as long as your overall motivation as in line with
the tournament's overall motivation (having fun, as expressed by
competition for the highest possible tournament standing). However,
if you don't wish to choose a style of play which resolves games within
the time limit, you will be penalized for that under the scoring system
and, IMHO, you should be.

> I described to you a deck that scored 2.5 vps and a game win in round
> 1, 1.5 vps in round 2 and 0.5 vps in round 3, and you told me (without
> knowing anything about the deck or why the game went to time) that
> this person should not have brought the deck to the tournament.

In my original reply to you, the use of the word "should" was intended
to convey "for purposes of winning the tournament" - not some kind of
moral value system or anything. The only thing you really told me about
your deck was that it tends to win after two hours and 15 minutes, a
period longer than the two hour time limit most tournaments use. Don't
conflate the sense of the generalized point I was trying to make: that
the scoring system deliberately penalizes slow decks for a good reason.
Your deck won one game and timed out two others. Of course, I can't
know the circumstances of the time outs with the above information so
please don't subsequently blindside me (again) with the inference that
I'm being overly judgmental with insufficient information, here. I'm
just trying to speak of general principals. If your deck which tends
to take longer to win than the tournament time limit was a contributing
factor to those two games timing out, then I think it's fair you should
penalized for it since the slow style of play robs other players of their
chance at getting game wins within the time limit. Hence, it becomes
an unfair penalty for them to draw you as an opponent.

You are, of course, free to choose such a deck anyway if you deem its
overall chance of success under the existing scoring system makes it
a good choice despite the penalties. But I see no reason to enhance
its value by increasing victory point rewards for timing out a game.
If anything, I would like to penalize such play even further.
Unfortunately, I can't think of any means of doing that without causing
some other undesirable effect. Until I do, I support continuation of
the existing system.

Fred

> guess the prior version was the same on this point (but I have been
> unable to find it).
>
> Although the half victory point time out rule always struck me as
> wrong, I cannot ever recall it being debated of justified.

I don't recall anyone questioning it either. I always took it as a
sign of agreement that 1) timeouts are bad; and 2) play which contributes
to timeouts (whether it be deckbuilding style or game play) is likewise
bad.

Norm is right about the game wins: they were instituted to discourage
dealmaking by players who tried to gain one or two VPs in exhange for
kingmaking another player, a style of play which frequently worked well
for those engaging in it but was found to warp the intent of the game
and rob it of its competitive balance. As I've said previously, the
current system has been arrived upon through a lot of hard experience.
Some of this may not be apparent to those who didn't live through it.

> At the time, there was no counting of game wins as primary criteria.
> Victory points were the primary criteria. If I were to guess, I would
> guess that the half-point rule was meant as a kind of imperfect
> attempt to ensure that players who won a game by the rulebook would
> get more points than those who merely scored a vp or two. Since it
> was possible to score a game win (per the rulebook) with only 2 vps, I
> would guess that someone decided it was unfair that a person who went
> to time with a single vp should earn the exact same result.

I always assumed the intent was to get players to recognize the time
limit and encourage them to attack with one another as opposed to
"turtling up" and merely surviving until time. Granting a player a
full VP for going to time rewards players who have no hope of ousting
their first prey equally with another player who is playing defensively
as a means of eventually winning the game. Granted, awarding both
players one half victory point does the same thing, but the above point
pierces the fallacy of trying to assert that scoring systems should
attempt to reward timed out game participants as closely as possible to
how they would be rewarded in a non-time-limited game. In truth, it's
impossible to do such a thing very accurately. So it should not be a
high priority.

Fred

Frederick Scott wrote:
> In general, you seem to think we should value consistency between
> tournament scoring and rulebook rules scoring and merely endeavor
> to find a tournament scoring system which rewards things as nearly
> as possible to non-timed play.

I would not say "as near as possible". For instance, where a 5-player
game goes to time with 4 players remaining, after A ousts B, my system
gives 2vp to Player A, and the other survivors 1 vp, but does not
award A a game win, despite the fact that he finished in the lead and
there is a logical basis for guessing that he is the most likely
winner. I still require two ousts for a game win. I deprive him of
his reasonable hope of a game win, but give him the fair vp value of
his game position as a consolation prize. This ensures that he has a
good incentive to finish the game, but is perhaps not quite so
frustrated when he fails.

Consistency between tournament scoring and rulebook scoring ensures
that players are competing with eachother and not with other tables.
Under the standard rules, every methuselah brings a vp with him to the
table. When any methuselah gets the better of another methuselah (by
ousting him) he takes his vp. One maximizes vp gain by besting each
opponent and avoiding being bested by any opponent, to the extent
possible. Ideally by ousting everyone, avoiding being ousted, thereby
getting 5 vp; but failing that, by any strategy that gets a lesser
number. Since you are competing against the other players at the
table, any vp point one gains is always at the expense of another
player.

By changing this dynamic, the current rules allow for situations where
one can maximize vp gain without getting the better of other opponents
at the table. One can get a full vp for oneself without taking a full
vp from an opponent. The extreme case of this, which I described for
Mr. Bakija, was one where a player calls an Ancilla Empowerment which
ousts all 5 players simultaneously. The result is a 5-way tie, in
which no player got the better of any other player in a meaningful
way. There motive, was to get a full vp instead of a half vp, but
they did not get this benefit at the expense of their opponents (who
each received the same benefit) But their opponents are the only
people they SHOULD be competing with. Instead, they are competing
with neighboring tables -- cooperating to ensure that the maximum
number of vps are distribued at their table.

Players SHOULD try to finish games, but should do so for the RIGHT
reason. The RIGHT reason to want to finish is that they want to get
the better of their opponents at the table. The WRONG reason is to
maximize the number of vps distributed at their table compared to
neighboring tables.

My system keeps the right reason for wanting to finish, and dispenses
with the wrong reasons. It keeps the number of vps at a table
steady. Under my system, if you want to gain a vp, you have to take
it from your enemy.

> You need to be aware that this is
> not all that high a priority in the tournament scoring system and

Well, if the Powers That BE never take my suggestion, then I will
suppose my concerns are not a priority for them.

> I don't believe it should be.

We may soon have to just agree to disagree. We are not making too
much progress. I understand what you are saying about there being

going to be any happier dying just because there is a half-price sale
at the funeral parlor. Under my proposal, just like under the current
system, a player who hopes to win generally needs to score at least
two ousts, and therefore needs to survive long enough to achieve this
-- which generally means surviving most of the game. Under my system
(as under the current system) any risks he takes are measured against
that hope of two ousts -- and not merely against the whole or half vp
he stands to lose.

> Tournaments feature time-limited games and they need to be played
> that way.

Yes, but, under my proposal they will continue to be played that
way.

> Players who play decks which can win given unlimited time but don't
> tend to resolve games before the tournament time limit SHOULD be
> penalized for that because such play unfairly robs other players
> who happen to draw them as opponents during the tournament of
> their chance to get game wins.

That's where we disagree. They have not unfairly robbed other players
of anything. Each player has no obligation whatsoever to help
opponents gain vps -- quite the reverse in fact. His job is (if
possible) to sieze a vp from each opponent and (if possible) to not
let any opponent sieze a vp from him.

Every vp you get should be siezed fair & square from another
methuselah who lost exactly what you gained. Putting a discount on
death to bribe players to let other players oust them is silly.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
<nys...@cs.com> wrote in message
