> Players SHOULD try to finish games, but should do so for the RIGHT
> reason. The RIGHT reason to want to finish is that they want to get
> the better of their opponents at the table. The WRONG reason is to
> maximize the number of vps distributed at their table compared to
> neighboring tables.

I assert that your definition of a "right reason" is arbritrary and
not particularly important. I also assert that the emphasis you've
chosen to place on conservation of victory points is misguided.
In practice, there's less harm in robbing tables of victory points
based on failure to resolve a game than in unduly rewarding the
failure to resolve a game. Were there a reliable means of
indentifying the exact party guilty of "causing" the time out (or
"the most guilty" to further play with the concept) then perhaps
it would be reasonable to take victory points away from that party
and give them to other players and conserve the total at one VP per
player. In truth, of course, that's hopeless. But it works
reasonably effectively (at least in the long run) to penalize each
surviving player in a timed out game in order to discourage
timeouts.

And it's total argumentative chicaery to turn this construction on
its head and claim a player can create victory points out of thin
air by avoiding this penalty. One does not "get a full VP for
oneself without taking a full VP from an opponent" when one _avoids_
a penalty. That is simply doing what you're supposed to be doing.
The Ancilla Empowerment example is odd but, like the rest of your
complaints, it's not a thing that causes a real, tangible problem.
It's just an oddity which could potentially be employed by a
player to extricate a table which was going to time from the worst
result (as a group) of all - albeit if no one finished with 2 VPs,
I note the table would still finish without the game win.

In fact, along the same lines and much more realistic before the
rule change to grant withdrawn players only 1/2 of a victory point
instead of a full one, groups of players would sometimes agree to
mutually withdraw. This actually happened from time to time -
you'd see players drawing, discarding, and declaring their turn
over in a second or so. In theory, one or more of the players
could then double-cross the deal when the victims had discarded
their entire libraries and that happened once in a Blue Moon
as well - though the deals were fulfilled in the vast majority of
the cases. But my point is, all this stuff happened without
compromising the spirit of the game too badly. In retrospect,
the rule change was probably an improvment because mutual withdrawal
schemes (which were the main thing affected by it) really weren't
desirable outcomes. And a freak universal-ousting Ancilla
Empowerment could theorectically be employed to the same effect but
it's not a real problem because players are unlikely to deckbuild
or play for such outcomes, so the problem is limited to slim
chance. (More likely to be used by a player who had no chance of
any VPs except through it's use - which would be an entirely
legitimate play AFAICS.)

>> You need to be aware that this is
>> not all that high a priority in the tournament scoring system and
>
> Well, if the Powers That BE never take my suggestion, then I will
> suppose my concerns are not a priority for them.
>
>> I don't believe it should be.
>
> We may soon have to just agree to disagree. We are not making too
> much progress. I understand what you are saying about there being
> (theoretically) a marginally higher incentive to go to time under my
> system, but I just don't see it making much of a difference in
> practice, for all the reasons I gave.

It's not marginal and it does make a difference. And your system
also penalizes the two-VP-and-ousted player in a non-completed game
of his chance at a game win which is not a penalty I think is
a good thing either. By way of turnabout, your concerns about
conservation of victory points absolutely baffle me. They seem
more like ideology than practical problem solving.

>> Players who play decks which can win given unlimited time but don't
>> tend to resolve games before the tournament time limit SHOULD be
>> penalized for that because such play unfairly robs other players
>> who happen to draw them as opponents during the tournament of
>> their chance to get game wins.
>
> That's where we disagree. They have not unfairly robbed other players
> of anything. Each player has no obligation whatsoever to help
> opponents gain vps -- quite the reverse in fact. His job is (if
> possible) to sieze a vp from each opponent and (if possible) to not
> let any opponent sieze a vp from him.

If you play a deliberate game with a slow developing deck which risks a
table time out before victory, your play unquestionably exports that risk
to your opponents as well. This unfairly robs your opponents - in
comparison to other players at other tables who are not playing in a game
with a slow developing deck. This is, perhaps, one of the major failings
in your point of view. To suggest players at a table are competing only
with one another and not with the other players at the other tables is
simply wrong, a result of an overly narrow construction of the situation.
You can only make the finals by placing in the top five of *ALL* players
at the tournament. So if one or more of your opponents at your table
cause(s) a greater than normal risk of a timeout at your table, it makes it
harder than it should be for your or anyone else to get a game win at your
table. This is a bad thing and should be penalized.

Fred

Okay, but more generally, my issue and point was that survival (for --
at the very least, a substantial portion of the game) is essential to
winning, and one creates a rather questionable dichotomy when one says
that the point of the game is to oust rather than to survive. To win,
you have to outlast at least some other players -- usually most of
them.

Had I mentioned withdrawal, for completeness, I might have pointed out
that (1) a withdrawer is a type of survivor, because he is never
ousted; (2) a withdrawer is still required to remain in the game long
enough to exhaust his library; and (3) a withdrawer is still required
to remain in the game longer than at least one other player in order
for his withdrawal to grant him any hope of a game win.

> A ousts B then C. E ousts A. E plays Gambit Accepted.
> Many turns later, E withdraws.
> A wins 2-0-0-1-1.

the table have been reduced from 5 to 4. I was unaware that any cards
had been printed that were capable of altering the ultimate number of
vps distributed.

But looking at the example (and looking up the card text), it appears
to me that A ties with E for two victory points. E gets 1 vp for
withdrawal and an extra 1 vp for not being ousted at the end of the
game.

I suppose one could argue that, since cards are burned upon
withdrawal, this prevents the Gambit from taking effect. But in this
case the withdrawal is simultaneous with the end of the game. If
ousting you does not burn your cards fast enough to prevent one's
predator from gaining the extra vp for ousting you, then withdrawing
should not burn your cards fast enough to prevent you from gaining
that last extra vp at the end of the game.

I can see that, when E withdraws BEFORE the end of the game, one vp
would go up in smoke and no player would get it. I'm not too happy
about this, because it seems to me that the number of vps to be
ultimately distributed at a table should never be altered.

I said something like this, although, really, the jist of what I said
was that the point of the game is to oust your prey, and while it is
good to survive, it makes sense to reward and incentivize ousting over
simply surviving. The current system of 1VP for ousting and .5VP for
simply surviving (as opposed to being the last person at the table,
which also gets 1VP, as it is generally a more significant effort to
be last person standing than to just not get ousted before time runs
out) does this--it rewards ousting your prey (with the standard 1VP)
in preference to simply surving till time runs out (with the .5VP).
Both of these are better than dying (0VP). As a result, the order of
preference for these events are:

1. Oust your prey. Get 1VP.
2. Don't get killed before time runs out. Get .5VP.
3. Get killed. Get nothing.

Which is a very reasonable order of desireablity of these events.

If you get 1VP for surviving till time runs out, it will often be more
attractive to simply wall up and hope time runs out than it will be to
try and oust your prey. Which is why it would be a bad idea to change
the .5VP fro survival to 1VP for survival.

-Peter

Messages.Author: Jeff Kuta
Messages.Body:
On Sep 23, 10:51 pm, nyst...@cs.com wrote:
> I have not been a regular poster here for a while, so forgive if the
> following issue has been discussed before. I am proposing a
> tournament scoring system that seems to be an improvement over the
> current one, and I am interested in feedback and counterarguments.
>
> THE PROPOSED SYSTEM
>
> Same as the current system, except:
>
> 1) No messing around with half victory points in uncompleted games.
> A player gets a full victory point for not being ousted (whether due
> to withdrawal or due to still being in the game when time is called).
> This means that for uncompleted games, just like completed games, the
> number of victory points distributed among the players equals the
> number of players in the game.
>
> 2) For uncompleted games, 3 victory points (including the one for not
> being ousted, if applicable) are required for a game win. For
> completed games, one can still get a game win with 2 victory points
> (on those very rare occasion when no-one else has 2 victory points).
>
> WHY IT IS BETTER
>
> 1) It is more accurate in predicting what the outcome of the game is
> likely to be if the game were played to completion (see, for instance,
> the example below).
>
> 2) It is less encouraging of the sort of fast-vote and fast-bleed
> decks that tend to dominate tournaments.
>
> AN EXAMPLE
>
> The following example seeks show why the proposed system is better
> than the current system in predicting game outcomes:
>
> In a five-player game, A (playing a fast, aggressive deck) ousts B &
> C, then runs out of steam and gets ousted by E. D and E remain in the
> game when it gets called for time.
>
> Under the current system, players A, B, C, D and E get 2, 0, 0, .5 and
> 1.5 victory points respectively. A gets awarded a game win, E takes
> second place.
>
> This result, however, is dead wrong under the original rules. The one
> thing we know for certain is that, under the original rules, it is
> impossible for A to win the game. The best he can hope for is a tie
> for first place (which is not a win).
>
> If the game is played to a finish, there are only 3 ways it can end,
> only 2 of which are even remotely likely, and NONE of which result in
> a win for player A. Either E will oust D, in which case E will have 3
> victory points and a game win, or else D will oust E, taking 2 victory
> points, and tying with A so that nobody takes a game win. The third
> possibility, withdrawal, results in 2 victory points for E (no matter
> who withdraws) which is also a tie game with no winner.
>
> If ANYONE in this called-for-time game should be granted a game win,
> it should clearly be Player E, since he is the only person who has any
> chance of winning it if it is played to a finish. Indeed, if we make
> allowances for the fact that a person who starts winning is likely to
> keep winning, his odds of emerging as winner may be greater than 50%.
> Player A should not get it -- he is only the most successful of the
> proven losers.
>
> The proposed system has a fairer result. The five players get 2, 0,
> 0, 1, 2. Nobody gets a game win and Players A and E tie for first
> place.
>
> We cannot know whether D will end the game with 0 vp or 2 vp, so we
> split the difference and give him 1 vp. We cannot know whether E will
> end the game with 1 vp or 3 vp, so we split the difference and give
> him 2.
>
> ANTICIPATING SOME COUNTERARGUMENTS
>
> 1. "The point of the game is to oust people, not to sit there and
> survive."
>
> If the point of the game is really that simple, it is only because the
> current tournament rules have made it so by devaluing survival. The
> rule-book says differently. The rule-book says that survival or
> withdrawal is worth as much as the ousting of a single prey. Of
> course, the rulebook requires that one do more than merely survive in
> order to win the game. In addition to survival, you will probably
> need to oust two prey to win a completed 5-player game (in rare
> situations, one prey ousted plus survival will suffice). So yes, you
> need to do more than survive to win, just as you need to achieve more
> than a single oust to win; but that does not mean that a single oust
> should be worth more than survival.
>
> Yes, the rules do require ousting, and should require ousting. The
> proposed system reflects those values accurately.
>
> 2. "The current system encourages all players to play quickly in
> order to maximize victory points for themselves as well as the whole
> table; your proposed system might give a player currently in the lead,
> or anyone in danger of being ousted, an incentive to stall."
>
> This is true to some extent, but the force of this argument is very
> much abated by the fact that game wins are the primary measure of
> tournament success, with victory point totals being used only as tie
> breakers. Under the proposed system, a game win is far more likely in
> a finished game than an unfinished one, and I think this is all the
> incentive for speed that is needed. If the game does not make
> substantial progress, then nobody gets a game win.
>
> And, although I agree that it would be better if games would finish, I
> also feel that there can be too much of a good thing. An excessive
> "hurry hurry hurry" atmosphere of tournament play does not necessarily
> make for a relaxing and enjoyable tournament experience.
>
> 3. "Long drawn out games are boring, and are one of the flaws of
> V:TES. It is good that tournament rules alter the game environment by
> encouraging people to design decks that have some hope of proving
> their worth within a 2 hour time limit."
>
> Personally, I rather like long, drawn-out epic games. I am
> nonetheless willing to assume, for the sake of argument, that long
> games are bad for V:TES.
>
> My response, again, is that the need to score a "game win" (rather
> than merely survive or score more victory points than anyone else at
> the table) is sufficient encouragement for people to design reasonably
> fast decks intended to make substantial progress (including oustings)
> within the 2-hour time limit.
>
> And whatever the hostility toward drawn out games, I cannot help also
> noting substantial hostility towards the sort of fast bleed/vote decks
> that tend to do well in tournaments. People bemoan the fact that they
> cannot bring to tournaments the "interesting" decks that they reserve
> for casual play.
>
> Seems to me that the system I propose is a suitable compromise,
> offering reasonable encouragement to decks that can demonstrate SOME
> progress within 2 hours, but not unfairly rewarding the fast weenie
> deck that scores two victory points before it runs out of steam and
> gets ousted.

I'm a little bit late to the thread, but after reading a few of the
posts, I got to thinking about the current scoring structure. I think
this proposal is fine, but what I did not like is that there are two
separate conditions for earning a game win--3 VPs if game goes to
time, 2 VPs if otherwise. I think that's just too messy so I thought
about an additional consideration which not only solves this problem,
but creates a significant incentive for finishing the game to its
natural conclusion:

Give the sole survivor 2 VPs at the end.

I haven't thought about all the implications of this, but I think on
the face of it, they're positive.

* A player who makes a single oust and survives earns 3 VPs and the
GW.
* Players have no incentive to make a 3/2 deal because it might end up
being a 3/3 deal with no GW.
* That extra survival VP makes everyone want to finish the game to its
conclusion because it is a bonus that can only be earned with a
complete game.

Jeff

> Or you make a positive incentive for finishing the games in a timely
> fashion, like giving the Sole Survivor an additional VP for being the
> true last man standing. :)

That's not the same thing, and its contribution towards resolving
games would be questionable. An extra victory point for being the
last man standing is an incentive towards being the last man standing -
only. This doesn't necessarily reward taking risks that well since
an ousted player would never receive the bonus. Likewise, a conservative
player might be in just as good a position as an aggressive player because,
although he is at disadvantage in that his play will frequently prevent
games from resolving, his play will tend to insure he will be around until
the end so when one _does_ resolve, he has a better than average chance of
being the one who receives the bonus. This is at least a somewhat
compensating advantage.

The current system, which just flat out penalizes play that makes it
harder to resolve games, is the better way - albeit still admittedly
flawed.

Fred

Certainly, Let's say I am in a hopeless position. It's down to the
last two players. The other player has two victory points. I have
one victory point. I am fairly sure I can make it to the time out, but
I could also make a mistake and get ousted. With your victory
conditions, what do I do?

1) Do I agressively throw myself at my predator to try and get 3 VP's
for the Game Win?
2) Do I play for time and deny the other player a Game Win, which is
smart for me because less game wins means it will be easier for me to
make the finals with any other games I can win in a tournament.

See here is where subtle favoritism creeps into your model. If I am
playing against a player from a rival playgroup, the I can stall out
figuring that improves not only my, but also my friends chances of
making the finals. If I am playing against a player from my playgroup
then I can make several "fumbles" and hand the game win off. There is
no incentive within the game to stay in it other than to spite other
players.

No judge will ever catch a player making bad plays for a friend, ever.

This is in further reply to XZealot, the Noble Archon of the Swamp, on
the subject of those two Evil Colluders who have split a 5-player
table between them, and who are not trying to decide what to do with
eachother.

Evil Colluder A has 2 ousts; Evil Colluder B has 1 oust. If each
player "plays to win" per tournament rules (meaning a player with no
hope of a game win should instead maximize victory points), the game
will go to time. This will grant A and B 2.5 and 1.5 vp respectively
under the current system, and 3 and 2 vp respectivly under my proposed
system.

On the other hand, B could throw the game to A, granting A a 4 to 1
victory. (Alternatively, A could throw the game to B, granting B a 3
to 2 victory).

This is the real difference between the two systems. Under the
current system, a colluder can hand 1.5 victory points to an opponent
at the cost of 0.5 vps to himself. Under my system, there can only be
a 1 for 1 exchange.

I think that most players, when faced with a situation where everyone
can be penalized by losing a half VP will take that choice rather than
risk losing it all and being ousted. Misery loves company. Somehow it
seems more fair when everyone gets the same penalty and no one gets
the bonus. There is lots of psychology to support this point of view.
I think this pessimistic mindset is built into the tournament scoring
system and discourages games from going to their full conclusion. I
tend to think of the scoring system for World Cup soccer which used to
only award 2 points for a victory and 1 for a tie and made for some
really boring games. There is a positive incentive now with 3 points
for a victory and teams will fight for those wins.

Adding the bonus VP for Last Man Standing is an attempt to address
this and encourage players to finish games entirely. It has another
small side effect of closing the gap between the worth of 4- and 5-
player tables since there are 5 and 6 VPs at stake instead of 4 and 5.
I don't think it would encourage walls to become the last man standing
because you only earn the VP if the table reaches its conclusion.

Jeff

solvable by modifying the scoring system for the most part. I think

While mutual withdraws are probably less common than regular timeouts,
it is partly because many (most?) players don't consider the absolute
difference between 1/2 and 1 VP to be significant. When you put then
in relative terms compared to the number of VPs required to win a
game, you can see the difference more dramatically.

I see the point your are illustrating taking it to the logical
conclusion, but I also agree that the process of reaching a game's
ultimate conclusion should play some part in its evaluation so each
oust should be worth something still. I suppose if enough people felt
that we should award 5 VPs for LMS that would make it very clear that
finishing a game is of paramount importance.

This makes me think of another alternate tournament scoring system
which we use for youth soccer here. Typically, two flights of four
teams play three opponents in a round robin earning points based on
performance. The top two teams from each flight then play cross-flight
in the championship and consolation finals.

For each game a team earns:
5 points for winning
2 points for tying
1 point for every goal scored (up to four maximum)
1 point for a shutout
-2 points for each red card (player sent off for discipline)

Thus, the maximum number of points earned per game is 10 (5 for
winning, 4+ goals scored, 1 shutout, 0 clean sheet).

This format does away with wins and losses entirely and converts them
to points. Most other soccer formats fall back to goal differential as
a tie-breaker but this one incorporates the number of goals into the
score per game. Something similar could be done with GWs and VPs and
LMS.

I realize that back in the day, VPs were all that mattered and that
system was eliminated in favor of what we have now. I don't want to go
back to that at all. Mainly, I just wanted to point out that if the
VEKN thinks that there are problems with tables timing out (could be
just a local phenomenon), there are other ways to provide incentives
to finishing up games. Tweaking scoring structure is the obvious way
to provide the proper incentives to players.

Jeff

5 player table: A ousts B and C with E's help. Then A lets himself be
ousted by E. Three things can happen now:

1) Game goes to time. Score (VEKN system) 2, 0, 0, .5, 1.5. Game Win
to A.
2) E ousts D. Score 2, 0, 0, 0, 3. Game Win to E.
3) D ousts E. Score 2, 0, 0, 2, 1. Tie Game (No Game Win).

Under my proposal, the surviving players in an unfinished game get an
extra half vp, so...

1) Game goes to time. Score (My Proposal) 2, 0, 0, 1, 2. E ties with
A.
2) E ousts D -- E wins
3) D ousts E -- D ties with A.

So actually, under my proposal, A's game win (in an unfinished game)
is foiled by the extra half-victory point granted to the survivors. 2
vp (ousts) + 0vp (non-survival) ties with 1 vp (oust) + 1 vp
(survival).

So even if I leave the Game Win requirements at 2 vp (allowing a Game
Win to a surviving player with a single oust -- providing no other
surviving player has an oust), the ousted player with 2 vp cannot
win.

Object of the Game

Your goal is to accumulate the most victory points by destroying the
influence held by rival Methuselahs. You accomplish this goal by using
your influence to gain control of younger vampires and using those
vampires to take actions to reduce the influence of rival Methuselahs.

1.2), the main currency of the game. When a Methuselah runs out of
pool counters, she* is bereft of influence and ousted from the game.

> don't think enough people see how far behind missing out on a GW

> table. Of course, some might consider this solution overkill for a

Obviously, from how I've argued my disputes with "nystulc", whoever this
person is, I have no love of ultraconservative play. But playing to
be LMS is simply not the same thing as playing to oust. In many cases,
I'm sure the same incentives would incentize both goals but in some
cases it would not. And even if I agreed with you about the clarity of
the incentives, I just don't think incentives are really the problem,
here.

>> > Adding the bonus VP for Last Man Standing is an attempt to address
>> > this and encourage players to finish games entirely. It has another
>> > small side effect of closing the gap between the worth of 4- and 5-
>> > player tables since there are 5 and 6 VPs at stake instead of 4 and 5.
>> > I don't think it would encourage walls to become the last man standing
>> > because you only earn the VP if the table reaches its conclusion.
>>

>

> that is precisely what gives you the bonus? Are you suggesting I'm
> discounting what negative effect this might have on game play toward
> an even more careful conservative game?

Um, in a word: yes.

> I think it would have quite
> the opposite effect and therein lies the disagreement.

OK. I stand corrected in that sense.

> Yes, we wouldn't have players necessarily racing out of the gate to
> earn their 3 VPs and then run out of gas. I don't see a problem with
> that.

I'm not sure I think there's a big problem with it. It bothers me
that IMHO it disincentizes situations where a person has to decide
between making a lunge for a second VP while fearing that the
lunge will ultimately get him ousted, even if he succeeds. You
can jigger with the various odds to decide how to treat it with
game theory: raise and lower the chance of succeeding with the
lunge, the chance the player will be ousted if the lunge fails,
and the chance the player will be ousted even if the lunge succeeds
and he has six more pool to work with. Ultimately, people in this
situation will tend to be more oriented towards being LMS instead
of getting ousts when and where they can. I note that it would not
rob the ousted guy with 2 VP of his game win if the game doesn't
not resolve, unlike nystulc's proposal. That makes your suggestion
superior to his in my eyes. But even so, game wins from being LMS
become worth relatively more (you get an additional VP along with
your LMS GW) and thus it's relatively more worth to pass up the
chance at a payoff from lunging for a second VP. I'm afraid that
makes it a loser as far as encouraging games to resolve, so thus
I'd be opposed to it.

> I seem to remember a (Swiss?) player posting that they design decks to
> take 2 VPs then merely survive so they'll get the Game Win without the
> game going to conclusion. That's a pretty poor attitude to take IMO,
> but you know, it can win with the current structure. Giving that
> little nudge to encourage players to fully finish might eliminate this
> sort of strategy from tournaments, or at the very least encourage
> aggressive players who do well at the start to keep the pedal to the
> metal and finish the game out entirely, rather than coast to the
> finish line with a lackey at their back.

I don't think so. It's a nudge, but I don't think it's hard enough
nudge in that situation. Someone with 2 VPs and the ability to
survive would be risking his GW to play over aggressively. Thus, I
think the extra VP incentive is not going to enter his thinking as
nearly as much as the person who has no GW and is just deciding
whether to lunge at a second - or even at a first - VP.

> I just don't believe there will be people out there trying to let
> their prey earn 3 VPs and then try to snag last man standing for a 3-3
> TIE with no game win.

No. Agreed, that scenario doesn't bother me. I'm not sure what brought
this up, however.

Fred

you.

Object of the Game

Your goal is to accumulate the most victory points by destroying the
influence held by rival Methuselahs. You accomplish this goal by using
your influence to gain control of younger vampires and using those
vampires to take actions to reduce the influence of rival Methuselahs.
Influence is represented by pool counters (see Equipment Needed, sec.
1.2), the main currency of the game. When a Methuselah runs out of
pool counters, she* is bereft of influence and ousted from the game.

*****AS METHUSELAHS ARE OUSTED, players earn victory points; the
winner is
the player with the most victory points at the end of the game *****

This is to encourage aggressive play and prevent overly defensive
strategies from dominating the game.

4) [2vps for a GW in a completed game versus 3vps in a game that timed
out] This is blatantly unfair to deny a player who has ousted 2
players the game win only because he was then ousted and the game went
to time. This overly punishes aggressive play and foils the original
intent of the designer to keep players acting aggressively against
their prey. It also creates a mechanic where other players can
engineer denying a GW to the player who has earned by timing out a
game.

leaving E & D to survive til time out] is the *only* situation where a
person who would get a game win under the current system would not get
one under mine.

There are exotic situations where one could get a game win under my
system where you could not have done under the current system. I
believe they all involve a player avoiding the half-point withdrawal
penalty of the current rules, in a finished game. For instance

A ousts B, A withdraws, an ancilla empowerment ousts the remaining
players simultaneously, A wins with 2, 0, 1, 1, 1 (he would have got
only 1.5 under the current system, denying him a game win).

> When a game doesn't go to time, someone else in the
> game should have gathered at least 2 VPs under the current system,
> anyway.

Yes, usually you need 3 vp to win. If no-one has scored an oust when
you leave the game with 2 vp (possible if you withdraw following an
oust -- except under the current system that gets you 1.5 rather than
2), then there is a possibility that the remaining players will tie 1,
1, 1 -- and you win (or would were it not for the half-point discount
on withdrawal).

But you left the game with 2 vp, and someone has scored an oust (by
ousting you) then there are NO situations (exotic or otherwise) that
can preserve the game win for you. An ousted player with 2 vps has no
hope of a game win whatsoever -- not even a theoretical one. This is
because 3 players have left the table, taking 2 vp with them, and the
remaining 2 players are fighting over the last 3 vp.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:


Correct.

The (basic) game doesn't reward you for "not be ousted" per se.
It rewards you for only three things:
1. your prey is ousted
2. being the last one left in the game.
3. successfully withdrawing.

(and note that 2 and 3 are mutually exclusive)

So "not being ousted" is actually only rewarded as "not being ousted when all
other players have been ousted or have withdrawn."

The current V:EKN tournament rules add a new reward: half a VP for not being
ousted when the time limit is reached (as well as reducing the reward for
successful withdrawal).

The basic rules exactly mimic an "ante" system, where each player antes a VP to
the pot (or to their position) at the start of the game to be awarded as above.

Maintaining that paradigm is definitely a good idea. I like the principle
involved in any effort toward that goal.

But there are other good ideas that compete with that goal, which is why, I
presume, the DCI implemented a reduced reward for time-outs (see the World Cup
parallel) which the V:EKN kept.

Sure. Of course, one could think of the latter two as two mutually
exclusive ways of "not being ousted" -- one determined at the end of
the game, the other before. In each case, the victory point is
granted when it is determined, for certain, that the player will never
be ousted.

> So "not being ousted" is actually only rewarded as "not being ousted when all
> other players have been ousted or have withdrawn."

Sure, except that one can think of withdrawal as an additional "not
being ousted" scenario, in which case, it would be more accurate to
say that "not being ousted" is only rewarded at the point in the game
where it can be determined that you will not be ousted.

> The current V:EKN tournament rules add a new reward: half a VP for not being

> successful withdrawal).

>
> But there are other good ideas that compete with that goal, which is why, I
> presume, the DCI implemented a reduced reward for time-outs (see the World Cup
> parallel) which the V:EKN kept.

Yes, but, originally, when the DCI implemented the reduced award, the
"Game Win" system was not yet in place. It is possible that the Game
Win system (which my proposal preserves) already serves whatever
function the DCI originally had in mind.

Imagine a 4 player game, where the last 2 players (A and C), each with
a victory point, duke it out. Under the former VEKN rules, each of
these players anticipates the following awards:

Time-Out Tie: +0.5 vp, +0.5 vp (total 1.5 vp, 1.5 vp)
Other Deadock (withdrawal): +1.0 vp, +1.0 vp (total 2.0 vp, 2.0 vp)
A ousts C: +2.0 vp, +0 vp (total 3.0 vp, 1.0 vp)

A player gets 4 times as much for winning as he does for tying the
game.

Imagine the same game under my proposal:

Time-Out Tie: +1 vp, +1 vp (total 2.0 vp, 2.0 vp)
Other Deadlock (withdrawal): +1, +1 (total 2.0, 2.0)
A ousts C: +2.0 vp & +1 gw (total 3.0 vp & 1 gw, 1.0 vp)

It is hard, under the current game win system, to measure the value of
a victory point versus the value of a game win. But if I assume that
a game win award is at least as valuable as 2 vps* then A is still
getting at least 4 times as much for winning as he is for tying the
game.

On the other hand, under the current VEKN system, which introduced the
game win system while keeping the half-point system (and also
introduces half points for withdrawals):

Time-Out: +0.5 vp, +0.5 vp (total 1.5 vp, 1.5 vp)
Other Deadock (withdrawal by A): +0.5 vp, +1 vp & 1 gw (total 1.5 vp,
2 vp & 1 gw)
A ousts C: +2 vp & +1 gw, +0 vp (total 3 vp & 1gw, 1 vp)

If we assume the game win award is (at least) worth 2 vp, we now have
a situation where the reward for winning is at least 8 times the
reward for a tie game. Whatever functions the win bonus serves, might
not this be overkill?

(Incidentally, under the current system one can have the bizarre
situation where a person caught in a deadlock with his opponent --
such as all vamps in torpor with no prospect of either player rescuing
them -- uses the deadlock-breaking mechanism of withdrawal to throw a
half victory point and a game win at his opponent at no cost to
himself).

* This seems reasonable -- even conservative. It is possible, in a 3
preliminary round tournament, for a person with 6 vp and 3 gws to beat
someone with 12 vp and 2 gws -- so it is theoretically possible to
have situations where 1 extra gw trumps 6 extra vps; an if you object
that this example hardly matters because both people are sure to make
the final round in any event, one still can have a situation where a
person with 2 vp and 1 gw beats someone with 6 vp and 0 gw -- 1 extra
gw trumping 4 extra vp. If you further object that 2 vp game wins are
rare, we can still have situations where a person with 3 vp and 1 gw
beats someone with 6 vp and 0 gw -- 1 extra gw trumping 3 extra vp.

That is not how an ante system works, at least not the way I learned
it. The ante is the cost of entering the game. You only leave the
table with your winnings. If you leave before the game is over then
you forfeit your ante. The ante is to keep players in the game and
create a value over which the game is fought. It is what the players
must risk to participate.

If, as you say, VTES is based upon the ante system, then a player does
not reclaim their ante at the end of the game, but only leave with
their winnings (earned VPs). I can't think of a game that uses the
ante system and a timing system other than VTES. As far as I know,
the only way to reclaim an ante is to win the game, in either VTES or
any other game.

>> ousted when the time limit is reached (as well as reducing the reward for
>> successful withdrawal).
>>

>> the pot (or to their position) at the start of the game to be awarded as above.
>>

>> involved in any effort toward that goal.
>>
>> But there are other good ideas that compete with that goal, which is why, I
>> presume, the DCI implemented a reduced reward for time-outs (see the World Cup
>> parallel) which the V:EKN kept.
>
> Yes, but, originally, when the DCI implemented the reduced award, the
> "Game Win" system was not yet in place. It is possible that the Game
> Win system (which my proposal preserves) already serves whatever
> function the DCI originally had in mind.

Yes, but the thing you don't explain is why this matters. If you comprehend that
the game win artifact was put into place to compensate for failings in the
previous (inherited-from-the-DCI system), you seem to accept that there were
reasons for making this change. Why then would you assert that the 1/2 VP
penalty could have been obsolesced at that moment but that no one would think to
eliminate it as the Game Win was instituted? Presumably, if it had become truly
obsolete, it would have been. It wasn't. This point exposes all this historical
conjecture for what I think it is: manufacturing a convenient justification.
"Ooops! See here, this should have done this in 2001 but they forgot!" We
didn't forget. I was one of the ones talking about the original table win
proposal back in 2001. Although a lot of different criteria were discussed at
the time, and although the tournament rule just magically showed up in the
2002 tournament rules without discussion as to who's proposal exactly was used
to create the final criteria for the game win (doesn't really matter -
it was as close to a collective act of creativity as I've ever seen in truth),
I can say that the criteria were being discussed in terms of number of _ousts_
required, with no one that I saw particularly felt like survival to the game's
end should make a difference. The main contention was over such nuances as,
"Should a table win be split if two players both scored 2+ VPs."

One critical point to consider in this discussion: With as much interest as there
was with fixing the perceived shortcomings of the system in 2001 and at various
periods since (Succubus Club eventually got updated and then eventually banned;
the two seat-switching cards likewise got banned), no one until you has ever
stood up and said, "Gee, it's a problem that people are getting penalized by
only getting 1/2 VP in timeouts." The tournament rules have even been changed
to make withdrawals equal in reward to time outs - rather than the other way
around - in that period. You seem to be quite unique in your perception that
this is a problem. It's certainly not because others are uninterested in the
subject.

Fred

If a game is unavoidably ended prematurely, presumably the remaining

> I can't think of a game that uses the
> ante system and a timing system other than VTES. As far as I know,
> the only way to reclaim an ante is to win the game, in either VTES or
> any other game.

In vtes, the winnings are awarded incrementally, in the form of
"victory points". By the time the game ends, the total winnings
awarded equals the number of players.

5 vtes gamblers come to the table, each placing a hundred dollar bill
in the pot. A ousts B. A grabs a hundred dollar bill from the pot
and puts it in his pocket. These are his "winnings" so far. $400
remain. A ousts C. A grabs another hundred dollar bill pot and puts
it in his pocket. $300 remain in the pot. E ousts A. E grabs $100
from the pot and puts it in his pocket. (A leaves, and goes home
with $200 in his pocket). $200 remain. E and D duke it out for the
next 2 hours, trying to win the money for themselves. Then,
unavoidable circumstances -- beyond anyone's control -- bring the game
to a forced and premature concludion -- the cops show up to arrest
them for gambling. E and D quickly split the pot between them, each
taking $100, and run out the back door. A similar result would have
occurred had they found themselves hopelessly deadlocked, and had
needed to resort to the withdrawal mechanism to end the game.

Perhaps, but it doesn't seem plausible.

Adding an extra 0.5 for time-out standing would certainly do nothing to address
the kind of deals and splits that the GW was added to address.

> Imagine a 4 player game, where the last 2 players (A and C), each with
> a victory point, duke it out. Under the former VEKN rules, each of
> these players anticipates the following awards:
>
> Time-Out Tie: +0.5 vp, +0.5 vp (total 1.5 vp, 1.5 vp)
> Other Deadock (withdrawal): +1.0 vp, +1.0 vp (total 2.0 vp, 2.0 vp)
> A ousts C: +2.0 vp, +0 vp (total 3.0 vp, 1.0 vp)
>
> A player gets 4 times as much for winning as he does for tying the
> game.
>
> Imagine the same game under my proposal:
>
> Time-Out Tie: +1 vp, +1 vp (total 2.0 vp, 2.0 vp)
> Other Deadlock (withdrawal): +1, +1 (total 2.0, 2.0)
> A ousts C: +2.0 vp & +1 gw (total 3.0 vp & 1 gw, 1.0 vp)
>
> It is hard, under the current game win system, to measure the value of
> a victory point versus the value of a game win. But if I assume that
> a game win award is at least as valuable as 2 vps* then A is still
> getting at least 4 times as much for winning as he is for tying the
> game.

At least, indeed. As VPs don't factor in at all except as a tie breaker for GW
ties, the GW is effectively worth as many VPs as you like.

> On the other hand, under the current VEKN system, which introduced the
> game win system while keeping the half-point system (and also
> introduces half points for withdrawals):
>
> Time-Out: +0.5 vp, +0.5 vp (total 1.5 vp, 1.5 vp)
> Other Deadock (withdrawal by A): +0.5 vp, +1 vp & 1 gw (total 1.5 vp,
> 2 vp & 1 gw)
> A ousts C: +2 vp & +1 gw, +0 vp (total 3 vp & 1gw, 1 vp)
>
> If we assume the game win award is (at least) worth 2 vp, we now have
> a situation where the reward for winning is at least 8 times the
> reward for a tie game. Whatever functions the win bonus serves, might
> not this be overkill?

No. The GW is supposed to serve exactly this function -- to shift the focus away
from counting (splitting) VPs back to the primary goal of the game: winning the
game (by achieving a plurality of VPs).

In the time-out case, the plurality is missed, so the reward is severely reduced.

> (Incidentally, under the current system one can have the bizarre
> situation where a person caught in a deadlock with his opponent --
> such as all vamps in torpor with no prospect of either player rescuing
> them -- uses the deadlock-breaking mechanism of withdrawal to throw a
> half victory point and a game win at his opponent at no cost to
> himself).

Giving a GW to another player is a cost.

> * This seems reasonable -- even conservative. It is possible, in a 3
> preliminary round tournament, for a person with 6 vp and 3 gws to beat
> someone with 12 vp and 2 gws -- so it is theoretically possible to
> have situations where 1 extra gw trumps 6 extra vps; an if you object
> that this example hardly matters because both people are sure to make
> the final round in any event, one still can have a situation where a
> person with 2 vp and 1 gw beats someone with 6 vp and 0 gw -- 1 extra
> gw trumping 4 extra vp. If you further object that 2 vp game wins are
> rare, we can still have situations where a person with 3 vp and 1 gw
> beats someone with 6 vp and 0 gw -- 1 extra gw trumping 3 extra vp.

True.

Back to the main:

As I said, maintaining the ante property of VPs is a solid goal.
The problem situation is the one of risk analysis, much the same reason that the
Edge was implemented (and the withdrawal rules). IMO, anyway.

Get A and C as you have above (1 VP each). Sometimes (perhaps frequently) it
will be that neither of them can get into a position to guarantee a no-risk path
to ousting the other. In order to scrabble for extra advantage, some risk would
have to be taken (risking being ousted and giving up the GW, not to mention the VP).

In the current environment, players face a VP penalty (in the ante sense, since
they will take back only a fraction of their ante upon a time out), providing an
impetus to take a risk (go forward).

In the pure ante environment (your proposal), the impetus is not there. The
player could risk a win (with an average chance of success at 50%) for an
expected outcome of 1 VP (.5 * 2VP + .5 * 0 VP; the GW is a wash at .5 * 1 + .5
* -1) or avoid the risk and bide time until the time out, again for an expected
outcome of 1 VP.

As opposed to an expected outcome of 1VP for risk-taking vs 0.5 VP for biding
time under the current system.

Is not the need go score a GW (which neither A or C have yet earned) a
far more effective incentive than a difference of a half vp? Even
those who have not earned a vp yet will be thinking of the GW, and
will want to score one oust as a first step to scoring two ...

I recognize a somewhat different mechanic might operate where a player
who has scored 2 ousts faces two remaining players with none. Here,
he has minimal incentive to go foreward, since he need only maintain
the status quo to preserve his GW at time out. Arguably, my proposal
gives him even less incentive to go forward than the current system.
But even here, I think the need for a GW will dominate his mind.
Maintaining the status quo is harder than it sounds. He faces two
hungry opponents who know they need to sweep the rest of the table to
gain that precious GW, and he knows that just one more oust will
cement his victory.

> In the pure ante environment (your proposal), the impetus is not
> there. The player could risk a win (with an average chance of
> success at 50%) for an expected outcome of 1 VP (.5 * 2VP + .5 * 0
> VP; the GW is a wash at .5 * 1 + .5 * -1) or avoid the risk and
> bide time until the time out, again for an expected outcome of 1
> VP.

You objected before -- perhaps correctly -- to my clumsy attempt to
combine the value of VPs and GWs. So let us look at the calculation
soley in terms of GWs.

He currently has 0 GWs. If he makes his risky move, he has 50% chance
of gaining a GW and no chance of losing a GW (since he cannot lose
what he does not yet have). If he does nothing, his expected outcome
is 0 GW. So the risky move is definitely a go at (.5 * 1) + (.5 * -0)
at an expected outcome of +0.5 GW.

> As opposed to an expected outcome of 1VP for risk-taking vs 0.5 VP
> for biding time under the current system.

But if the GW system has had its intended effect, and he is now
minimally interested in VPs except as a means of getting GWs, how much
will the player really be interested in such calculations?

>

>3 would be better yet for each. And so on until LMS is the new GW (5
>would do it).

Although there is a reducto ad absurdum problem if you follow the
motivation thoroughly, I do like the fact that this suggestion means
that a predator and prey won't do a deal to get the game win by doing a
3-2 split and rolling over once the game win has been gained.

This sort of thing is the one annoyance left after the "all deals are
off at 2 plays" change - because the player with the game win doesn't
need the "permission" of a pre-existing deal, as she can win in any way
she chooses.

I'm not sure if an extra VP for LMS would have any adverse effects on
other situations, but I do like its effect on this situation.

Let me see...

- a sweep gets 6 VP, which is fine

- a current "2-1, fight it out at the end" deal turns into 5-1 (instead
of 4-1) or 4-2 (instead of 3-2), which seems fine

- a deck that gets to the endgame without any prior VPs and survives
would get 3VP, which could tie with the 3VP of its prey, which
might be awkward

- a back-ousting !Malk deck could split a table 3-1-1-1-0, rather than
2-1..., which seems no particular bother

- a Peter Bakija-esque "Destroy prey, get LMS" could get 4 vs the other
2 VP, which is reasonable. But if it only got LMS, it could be
a 3-3 tie.

Now, we could resolve the awkward "sit on your hands, and survive the
endgame" issue by changing it to: "The last man standing gets 1VP if she
has zero VP prior to the final oust (or simultaneous ousts), or 2VP if
she has more than zero VP prior to the final oust (or...)."

That would give us:

- 6 VP (fine)
- 5-1 or 4-2 (or 4-1-1-0-0) (fine by me)
- 3 (prey) - 2 (Last Man Standing - no VPs prior to the one-on-one
endgame)
- 2-1-1-1-0 for the !Malk going backwards, which would still be a GW
- 4-1-1-0-0 or 4-2-0-0-0 for the Bakija "destroy prey, get LMS" combat
style, but if it can't get an oust of its prey prior to
the endgame, it gets 2VP for getting LMS (and its prey could get
the other 3VP and win)

There are doubtless other cases I'm not considering - such as a withdraw
from someone else on the table doing something odd, or Gambit Accepted -
and I'm *only* considering completed games (because LMS doesn't matter
in uncompleted games).

Is this a desirable change?

Okay, but if the result of the above is a complete wash, completely

the same logic, the risk incentivizing rewards offered by the VEKN vp
allocation system are equally illusory. Your 50% fear of losing half
vp (compared to time out) is exactly balanced by a 50% hope of costing
your opponent the exact same thing. Your 50% hope of earning 1.5 vps
(compared to time out) is exactly balanced by your 50% fear of
granting your opponent the exact same thing.

I think the answer, in both cases (GW awards, and VP awards under
VEKN), lies the following two facts: (1) we are not dealing with a
zero sum game, and (2) this is a broader competition that extends
beyond this individual game. Because he is competing not only with
the player at his table, but also the players at other tables, he has
an incentive to maximize the GWs and VPs earned at the table, in the
hope that he shall be the one to win them. The risk taking described,
therefore, can be thought of as a cooperative enterprise to maximize

will earn them, to ensure that the winner(s) of this table will be
competitive with the winner(s) of other tables.

Many people play extra carefully because they do not want to be
ousted. Decks can be designed this way. Players may be ultra cautious
during their turns taking extra time during all the phases. Some
people even come to tournaments with decks they have never played
before and may still be learning what the cards do. When this happens,
it is not unusual for five players to still be contesting a game
90-119 minutes on.

Since each turn becomes more precious as the clock ticks away, people
set themselves up to lunge and try to win at the end because they full
well know the game cannot come to a complete conclusion. Sniping for a
VP or two at the last minute can be a successful strategy.

I think a preferable way to deal with this would be to award bonuses
for a complete game rather than just penalizing everyone when it might
not really be everyone's fault for a time out.

Jeff

Looking at the current posted rules online, I see this, with no
mention of "time-out" at all. "The game continues until only one
Methuselah is left." Was there something in the original basic rules?
I don't recall.

9. Ending the Game
9.1. Victory Points
When a Methuselah runs out of pool counters, she is ousted from the
game. If you are ousted, all the cards you control are removed from
the game. Any of your opponents' cards you control are returned to
them at the end of the game. Any of your cards controlled by other
Methuselahs remain in play as normal (see The Golden Rule of Card
Ownership, sec. 1.3). The game continues until only one Methuselah is
left. You get a victory point whenever the Methuselah who is your prey
is ousted (no matter how or by whom your prey was ousted). You receive
an additional victory point if you are the last player left. At the
end of the game, the winner is the player with the most victory
points, even if she has been ousted. Along with a victory point, you
gain six pool from the blood bank when your prey is ousted.
EXCEPTION: If a player is ousted at the same time that her prey is
ousted, the player gets the victory point but does not gain 6 pool.

When your prey is ousted, the next Methuselah to your left (the ousted
Methuselah's prey) becomes your new prey.

9.2. Withdrawing from the Game

If you have exhausted your library and begin your turn with less than
a full hand, you have the option of withdrawing from the game. To
exercise this option, you must announce your intent to withdraw during
your untap phase. For the withdrawal to succeed, you must meet the
following conditions:

* None of your minions enter combat until your next untap phase.
* None of your minions lose (or spend) any blood until your next
untap phase.
* You do not lose (or spend) any pool until your next untap phase.

If on your next untap phase you have met these conditions, then you
successfully withdraw. The withdrawal fails if you lose a single pool
or blood, even if you gain enough to make up for the loss.

If you successfully withdraw, you receive one victory point to add to
any victory points you have already gained. Your predator does not get
a victory point or any pool for your withdrawal.

Jeff

I cannot see a meaningful distinction between a punishment for not
finishing and a reward for finishing. As you know, my proposal wants
to eliminate the current vp punishment for not finishing (reward for
finishing), and I am opposed to adding any additional punishments for
not finishing (rewards for finishing).

However, the "no GW" punishment for not finishing should be retained.
I believe the game win system, which is far more likely to grant a
game win in completed games, is an adequate award and incentive for
finishing. I think it has been largely successful in shifting the
focus from vps as an end in themselves, and that vp-based incentives
for risk taking are no longer likely to influence player behavior.

an important - and fun - aspect of Jyhad.

conjunction with a bonus VP for Last Man Standing.

>

My main bone of contention is how games often, in my experience (and
this is key as SF is notorious for slow, cautious, talkative
play...and I'm as guilty as anyone) slows to a crawl during the last
20-30 minutes while people set the game up for a last second stab at
the GW, even if three players still remain when time is called. That's
just not very satisfying and I think more can be done to encourage
games to finish.

Maybe I'll just have to play faster and nag my table mates to do the
same. ;)

Jeff

should be preserved, and survival rewarded ... but with only 1 vp.

propose that your incentive change the indentity of the game winner.

balanced once again, and the loopholes simply would not be there for
them to exploit. But I do not know what sort of unethical behavior
you have in mind.

Since my "scoring tweak" is intended to restore the setup of the
original rules, which is a zero sum game where exactly x players
compete for exactly x vps, your suggestion is DEFINITELY inconsistent
with my scoring tweak. It violates the whole principle on which it is
based.

In which case, the GW is awarded to the player who did the most to
finish the game. If the other two losers, who ousted nobody, do not
like it, then they can go ahead and try to sweep the rest of the table
before time out. Let THEM finish the game. Its the only way they can
get a GW.

Seriously, I am not about to lose sleep over a game, like the one
above, going to time. I can think of only two reasons to be
dissatisfied:

1) because of the suspicion that one of the other players would have
won if given enough time, and

2) because of the players feel cheated because their table was

Sorry dude. I think it's a bad idea.

My position on encouragement of risk taking is precisely this: The
Game Win system encourages risk taking. It does it in a FAR FAR more
powerful way than the VEKN vp allocation discount ever did, and does
so without distorting the game as Garfield designed it. I am
enthusiastically in favor of the Game Win setup, precisely because I
believe it has this effect.

Early rounds of World Cup Soccer incentivize risk taking by giving 3
points for a win and 1 for a draw. The VEKN system tried to
incentivize risk taking by offering (if the conditions were right) a
half point for a draw and 2 for a win (or 1 vs 4). But the GW system
offers NOTHING for a draw, except lousy tie-breaking victory points --
if you want a game win , you've got to go for the gusto.

The risk-taking lure of a game win manifests itself far earlier in the
game than the risk taking lure of that final game-ending oust. Two
outs puts you in the running for a GW. Once you have achieved that,
other players know they can win only by finishing the game.

Meanwhile (in my opinion) the VEKN vp allocation system is obsolete.
The measley vp bribe it offers has virtually no effect on player risk
taking. Player motivations are now completely overshadowed by the
hope of gaining, or the fear of losing a game win -- and the earning
of vps has properly become a means to that end. The skewed vp
allocation system has ceased to be part of the solution. The main
effect it has is to increase player frustration when their games go to
time. It's tendency to increase player frustration in time out games
far outweighs any tendency it has to prevent them.

Meanwhile, the VEKN vp allocation system continues to have a number of
minor, subtle, distorting effects on the game.

OK. If that's the extent of what you meant, then I'd say you
overlooked how what that could be taken in a completely different
way in that context. "Rewarding", "incentizizng", "punishing", "de-
incentizing" (or "disincentizing" - I think we're making up words at
this point) are all concepts that work equally well in the postitive
and in the negative. If one changes the scoring rules in some way which
lessenes the risk for getting ousted, that also promotes the reduction
of players which leads to the end of the game. One you missed,
apparently. Ousting can be incentived to a greater degree relative to
survival (it does not make sense to use the word "more" as if we could
compare the incentives of the two acts to one another directly; all we
can do is judge how the incentives have changed from one set of
scoring rules to the next) by reducing the punishment for not surviving
as well as by increasing the reward for ousting. Either one encourages
more risk-taking. "Increasing the reward for letting oneself be ousted"
sounds like a slanted way of describing the former. It does not sound
all that much to me like self-ousting, transferring out, or suicide.

That said, I don't suppose there's any point to sitting around sniping
about it. Yes, I agree, people should not be given reason to do things
which cause their own oust merely to reduce the number of players in the
game. However, making lunges to oust _another_ player often has that
side-effect, and it could be reasonable to reduce the punishment for not
surviving. I have no proposals to do so relative to the existing system.
But this is another reason why the 1/2 VP penalty for going to time makes
sense: it reduces the penalty for not surviving in such a game from 1 VP
to 1/2 VP, which makes the act of taking a lunge to cause another player's
oust at the risk of suffer one's own oust look relatively better. Notice,
however, it _also_ can be framed as "rewarding letting oneself be ousted"
in that it reduces the disincentive for getting ousted.

Fred

The Game Win is a powerful incentive. Unfortunately, for every person
at the 5-player table who eagerly wants to sweep the table, there are
4 other people at the table who want to stop him. Four dreams of
glory are inevitably shattered, and sometimes, 5 dreams are shattered
as well. Some of these frustrated losers will be philosophical about
their defeat, but inevitably, some will want to blame the system or
their fellow players and howl for a solution that is not needed.

> Whether
> there's too much, just enough, or not enough risk taking is, in the
> end, debatable.

Many players who fail to oust will always feel that their prey didn't
take enough risk. Many dissatisfied players who fail to win will
feel the desire to blame something or someone other than themselves.

I personally see no reason to believe that the tournament system is
not working. Inevitably, during the end of each tournament, a great
many players have scored ousts and game wins. A great many of these
games even finished within the two hour time limit -- or so I've
heard. The ones with the most game wins and (then) the most ousts get
to play in the finals. What reason do we have to suspect that these
decks and players are not the best decks and players -- the ones that
deserve to play in the finals? Why should we listen to the whining
of all the frustrated losers who want to blame their defeat on their
fellow losers, and howl for a solution that is not needed? If these
frustrated losers really believe in the risk taking they preach, how
come they themselves managed to survive a whole two hours without
scoring a single oust? Where was their courage? Why didn't their
decks contain a little less defense and blood gain, and a little more
forward power. Maybe if they practiced courage, instead of preaching
it, they would win more often.

> But I think you've gotten responses from at least a
> few of us who it as inadequate, if anything.

I'm sorry, you all of you have only managed to convince me that my
proposal is a good one. You see, I don't just count the number of
objectors. I take a look at what they have to say, and see if it is,
in my humble but unhesitant opinion, worthwhile.

> > Meanwhile, the VEKN vp allocation system continues to have a number of
> > minor, subtle, distorting effects on the game.
>

> But what defines "distortion", exactly, save for your truth-by-blatant-
> assertion reasoning?

If you were really interested in my answer to that question, you would
not have asked it in that way.

> And why should we care about this, in practical terms?

Since you apparently don't care, why bother me with such questions?

> Failure to conserve victory points does not a distortion (or an evil) make.

"Failure to conserve victory points" as you call it, is causing what I
arbitrarily consider to be subtle distoritions in the arbitrary rules
and arbitrary victory conditions of the arbitrary game of Jyhad as
arbitrarily designed by that arbitrary dude Richard Garfield, a game I
happen to rather like.

Banning Jyhad and forcing everyone to play Snakes and Ladders instead
does not an Evil make, unless you happen to arbitrarily prefer Jyhad.

> It's this repeated failure to justify your ideas about how you think a
> scoring system should look in terms of the practical goals that players
> really care about which robs it of any impetus.

Of course I cannot provide some kind of ultimate justification for my
preferences. Neither could anyone. I like Jyhad, have been playing
it for years, and have ideas about what I like about the game as
defined by the standard rules. I assume some common ground or common
values with at least some other players who also like the game of
Jyhad. I have nothing to say to those who prefer Tennis.

It is your demand for some Ultimate Justification for my values that
invalidates your Heckling. It is a cheap shot, that no reasonable
critic would make.

It is also, by the way, a cheap shot to taunt an outnumbered opponent
with the fact that he does not have the time to respond to each and
every one of his heckler's attacks. How much time do you think I have
on my hands?

> > Dude, I am not on the design team. But of course, I believe my system
> > will make things BETTER. If the design team does not buy my
> > arguments, you have nothing to fear.
>

> I sure hope I have nothing to fear from what's been presented so far.
> I do not believe I do.
>

> > (As for our powers of prediction, I am tempted to remind you of a
> > debate we had long, long ago ....)
>

> I'm afraid you have the advantage on me. I am quite aware that I have
> not been right about a lot of the things I've said here. On the
> other hand, in retrospect, I seem to have gotten lucky at least once or
> twice as well.

I had a strange sense of deja vu when I showed up here, and saw you
and Peter Bakija take me on. So I did a goodle search. The first
thing that came up was both of you (and especially you) vigorously
trying to convince me that disciplineless concealed weapon, if
printed, would be a broken card. I remember being sorely outnumbered
then too. Which is precisely why I am not impressed by the numbers
arrayed against me now.
