Frederick Scott wrote:
> <nys...@cs.com> wrote in message

> > If it is, the vp incentive adds nothing to it.
>
> It surely must add something [...]

I'll revise that to "virtually nothing" or "almost nothing".

> [...] or there would no reason to have it [...]

Originally, when vp's were the primary scoring reward of tournaments,
the risk incentivizing effect was far more substantial. Not so now.
In almost all situations where the reward might be a motivating
factor, it is eclipsed by the Game Win.

> [...] and,

> having it, no reason to quibble over its form.

There are at at least two reasons to quibble, regardless of its
ability to risk-incentivize:

1) Despite it's minimal-bordering-on-nonexistent inability to
contribute in a meaningful way to making games end earlier, it
nonetheless increases player frustration and dissatisfaction when,
inevitably, some games do go to time.

2) By subtracting half victory points from some players but not
others, the current system alters the identity of the game winner in
ways that are inconsistent with the values of the original scoring
system

> I do think we're
> mostly in agreement that the game win is, by far, the most powerful
> part of the incentive.

Well, that's good, anyway.

> >> But I think you've gotten responses from at least a
> >> few of us who it as inadequate, if anything.
> >
> > I'm sorry, you all of you have only managed to convince me that my
> > proposal is a good one. You see, I don't just count the number of
> > objectors. I take a look at what they have to say, and see if it is,
> > in my humble but unhesitant opinion, worthwhile.
>
> Well, OK. I stand by your right not to count numbers. I frequently
> take unpopular positions myself. (Displays "Ask me about the screwed up,
> pointless, and stupid non-rating sytem!" button.) But I wonder what
> anyone might have said that could convince you of a thing?

Don't know until I hear it. My opinions have modified somewhat, or
developed, since starting on this NG, and I have incorporated some
ideas. However, I am still convinced my proposal is a good one.

> You don't
> seem interested in anyone's actual tournament experiences.

Well, I am happy to listen to any stories anyone wants to tell.
However, before anyone starts shooting, I should warn about my general
attitude toward two types of stories:

First:

If your story is about tournament finalists going to time in the final
round because they know they are ahead and want to win the tournament,
and, therefore, have no interest in a "game win" as such, or no
interest in gaining extra points, as long as they do better than
anyone else at the table and walk away with the prize loot, then the
sort of risk incentivizing rules we have been discussing will have no
effect upon them. As in soccer, this sort of risk incentivization can
only work in preliminary rounds.

Second:

Best I can see, the tournament system is working fine, meaning that at
least five players (and, I think, quite a lot more than this) have
scored a sufficient number of Game Wins and/or victory points over the
course of 2 hours in each of the preliminary rounds that the judges
have little or no trouble making an objective and reasonably
meaningful determination of who those 5 top players are. Judges are
never (as far as I know) placed in a position of saying "All 5 tables
went to time in all 3 rounds with all 5 tables remaining and everyone
has no GWs and 1.5 vp each. So who the hell do we pick for the
finals?"

Naturally, these 5 finalists are generally perfectly happy with the
results, even when (as is often the case) some of their games went to
time. The disatisfied ones, naturally enough, are the majority -- the
20 people who did not make the final -- who likely had their games go
to time at least as often -- and perhaps or probably more often --
than the finalists did. Many of the latter will be philosophical and
blame their bad showing on bad play and/or bad luck and/or the tough
quality of the competition, and simply vow to try do better next
time. Predictably though, at least some others will blame their
failure on their fellow players and/or on the system, and loudly
assert that they would have gotten into the finals (and no doubt, won
the tournament as well) if only that damned newbie with his wall deck
had gone forward and not played so damned slow and not so stubbornly
refused to be ousted, and not slowed down everyone else.

Such stories, even if there is alot of truth do them, do not prove the
system is not working. Good luck and bad luck and blind guesswork as
to what sort of opposition you may face are all part of the game. The
tournament winners had just as much chance as the frustrated loser did
to be seated next to the newbie with the wall deck -- and most likely
*did* sit next to him at some point during the 3 preliminary rounds.
Notwithstanding, these tournament winners still came out ahead of the
frustrated loser. If the finalists tended to have more success in
finishing their games before the time limit -- maybe that's just
because they are better at ousting their prey.

If one expects gripings from unhappy losers even in a well functioning
system, how can such gripings prove that time outs are a serious
problem?

> The one
> experience you've offered for us makes me think this is more about
> _you're_ being frustrated that decks prone to timeout tend to get
> slightly penalized by it and would rather change the scoring system than
> change your style of play to adapt. That's OK, if true - there's nothing
> wrong with proposing a change you think would make tournaments more fun.

I have a variety of decks, and I don't want to be unduly influenced
towards my fastest ones. If I did that, (and if everyone followed my
example) the game would merely become a boring bleed race. So yes --
it my deck does well enough in the game win department, I don't want
it penalized in the victory ponts department.

> But it makes me suspicious that there's nothing behind this purist
> advocacy of conservation of victory points you espouse.

Earlier, LSJ pointed out to me that errata was issued on the card
"Gambit Accepted" -- solely and precisely because the rules team
wanted to, as you put it, conserve victory points. I am therefore
somewhat reassured that this preoccupation is not entirely unique and
peculiar to me alone.

> People don't make deals to manufacture victory points in tournaments.

They did. Most famous were the cooperative withdrawal deals in the
earlier VEKN rules -- directly motivated by the failure to conserve
victory points, and the motive to maximize the table's vps through
cooperation. By "fixing" this problem, the VEKN caused, for the first
time, a distortion of the victory conditions as applied to completed
games.

> They can't.

They still can (even if illegal). Two deadlocked players can agree to
toss a coin or roll a dice to see which of them will withdraw and
surrender a game win to the other -- and unlike a similar agreement to
forfeiture, this does have any vp cost to the loser of the dice
role.

> There's no reason for them to.

Players collude for all kinds of reasons. Colluders are the players
with the most power to end games. Colluders, therefore, gain the most
benefit from any game-ending incentives.

> And you have no anecdotes and very little
> but conjecture to suggest any good practical reasons to worry about it.

I have given my reasons.

> So all we're doing is quibbling over whether timeouts should be slightly
> penalized or not.

My position was never that simple, since my proposal *does* tend to
penalize time outs -- the natural way -- by tending to deny them game
wins.

> You're not likely to be convinced they should if you
> think they shouldn't. Nor are you likely to convince guys like Jeff or
> myself that they shouldn't. So...end of story, AFAICS.
>
> >> > Meanwhile, the VEKN vp allocation system continues to have a number of
> >> > minor, subtle, distorting effects on the game.
> >>
> >> But what defines "distortion", exactly, save for your truth-by-blatant-
> >> assertion reasoning?
> >
> > If you were really interested in my answer to that question, you would
> > not have asked it in that way.
>
> Well, actually I am interested but it has been my observation that you don't
> have an answer to it. If you had, you'd have offered it up by now. In theory,
> opponents in the same game could make deals to manufacture victory points
> but the thing is, they have no reason to in practice. So why else should
> we care that victory points aren't conserved? I can't think of any reasons
> and you won't give any.

I have given reasons. You discount my reasons for reasons of your own
as to why you don't care about my reasons (you don't think the values
by which I define "distortion" matter -- etc. etc.) -- which is your
right to do. Problem is, having dismissed my reasons from your mind
for reasons of your own, you then go on to accuse me of not having
offered reasoning or analysis or examples to support my posision --
which is entirely false -- and then use this false claim as a basis
for further undue speculation about my motives. By the way, earlier
in this thread, you admitted that you had not read all my posts in
this thread, but (it seems) mainly just my responses to you
personally. I wonder -- did you correct this oversight before making
the above accusation? Because you really ought to have, I would
think.

> So, yes, the real reason to make that comment was to spotlight that your
> complaints are based in theory with no basis in real world problems - other
> than increasing the chances of making the finals for slow-developing decks.
>
> >> And why should we care about this, in practical terms?
> >
> > Since you apparently don't care, why bother me with such questions?
>
> Ah, but I _do_ care. That's the problem. I don't believe you do.

Well, being called a liar isn't exactly amusing for me, now is it --
especially after all the effort I have put into defending my
position.

Fine -- I will give you some distortions, most of which I have alluded
to elsewhere in thie thread. Note that I am aware that you have
already dismissed my examples for reasons of your own. I am aware,
that you may not accept my underlying ideas as to the intent behind
the original rules. You may not accept my view that Garfield's intent
in rewarding withdrawal and last man standing was simply to reward
survival (keep a victory point for not being ousted) and that the
reason he grants this award at the end of the game or upon withdrawal
is because that is the point at which it can be determined that the
player will not be ousted. Nonetheless, those are my views and
underlying assumption. With that in mind, the scoring paradigm is as
follows:

Ousted Non-Ouster: 0 vp
Live Non-Ouster: 1 vp
Ousted Single-Ouster: 1 vp
Live Single-Ouster: 2 vp.
Ousted Double-Ouster: 2 vp.
Live Double-Ouster: 3 vp.
Ousted Triple-Ouster: 3 vp
Live Triple-Ouster: 4 vp
Ousted Quadruple-Ouster: 4 vp (requires simultaneous ousts).
Live Quadruple-Ouster: 5 vp.

"Live" means "Never Ousted" (withdrawn, last man standing, or by
extension ... alive at time out).

So the formula is always 1 point per oust plus 1 point for "never
ousted". It is a zero sum game where the ousted player loses exactly
what his predator gains.

Note that, for the first examples below, I assume that the award for
successful withdrawal is still 1 vp. At the end, I discuss withdrawal
distortion under the newer VEKN rules

THE OUSTED DOUBLE-OUSTER vs THE LIVE SINGLE-OUSTER:

Under the paradigm of the standard rules, an ousted double-ouster has
the same worth as as Live (withdrawn or remaining) single-ouster.
Both earn 2 vp in a completed game -- often resulting in tie games.
The VEKN rules alter ("distort") this result by throwing the game to
the ousted double-ouster by penalizing the Live single-ouster with a
half vp penalty. Moreover, it applies these values inconsistently,
since it sometimes gives the Live single ouster his full 2 vps,
resulting in the tie from the standard rules. In a 4 player game, or
in a completed 5 player game, the ousted double-ouster, the withdrawn
single-ouster and the remaining single ouster receive exactly equal
credit, resulting in a tie. But in an uncompleted 5 player game the
ousted double ouster is declared winner, solely because of the
presence of a player who, under Garfield's scoring paradigm ought to
be irrelevant to the score of the other 4 because he has neither
ousted nor been ousted. This also creates a bizarre situation where
this irrelevant 5th player can deny the Game Win to the ousted double-
ouster by successfully withdrawing from the game. But why should the
withdrawal of a player affect the relative final scores of the
remaining 2 players? Under the standard rules paradigm, a withdrawn
player simply walks away from the table, taking with him the vp he
brought to the table, and leaves the remaining players as they were.

In this context, I mentioned to you specifically the possiblity that
the leading remaining player (the one who oused the double ouster)
might let himself be ousted (at a cost of a half victory point to
himself) to ensure that there was no game win for the remaining two
players at the table. You objected that this was illegal (you were I
suppose correct -- it violates the rule mandating maximization of
one's own victory points when one is without hope of a game win).
You nonetheless conceded that this rule was unenforceable. But it is
the distortions of the VEKN vp allocation system that have created
this illicit opportunity that depends upon an unenforceable rule for
its prevention. Eliminate the distortions (as my proposal does) and
one eliminates the illicit opportunity.

THE OUSTED SINGLE-OUSTER vs THE LIVE NON-OUSTER:

This works the same as the example above. It seems less important,
because the difference has no chance of affecting a game win. On the
other hand, the difference may large in the frustrated loser's mind
because it is a 50% discount from what he would have otherwise
gotten. He may have fought a long hard 2-hour battle, only to get
half as much as a player who died early in the game. Once again, the
award is applied inconistently: 4 player game -- A ousts B; A ousts
C; game goes to time; D gets 0.5 victory points. But if A ousts B; A
ousts C, A withdraws; D gets 1 victory point. Why should D, who did
nothing in either scenario -- except survive -- get a half point
depending on D's behavior here.

THE LIVE DOUBLE-OUSTER:

Not a critical issue, since he gets a game win under the current
system. Under Garfield's paradigm, he should get 3 vps, but in
unfinished games, the current system reduces this to 2.5. Again this
is applied inconsistently, for the Live double-ouster gets 3 vp in
completed games (a not-uncommon scenario). People who claim that the
extra half vp is a "reward for completing the game" would seem to be
wrong. In both situations, the ousted double-ouster has made exactly
the same contribution to completing the game -- he has ousted two
players. Giving him an extra half point for completing the game is in
fact to reward him for the game-ending contributions of other
players. For example, a player with one oust may end the game as an
Live double-ouster by eliminating the final player. He gets his extra
half point, apparently, because one or more of his victims ousted two
players. Or an Live double-ouster may face off against a single
player -- if the game goes to time the Live double-ouster gets 2.5 vp,
but if the final opponent withdraws -- and Live double-ouster lets
him, then the Live double-ouster gains the extra half vp for the final
opponent's behavior.

THE LIVE TRIPLE-OUSTER

Analysis is similar to the above, except that in a 4-player game, he
always gets 4 vp, and not 3.5. In a 5-player game the presence of a
do-nothing 5th player, who manages neither to oust nor be ousted,
costs him a half vp, despite the fact that his own accomplishments are
exactly the same. (As always, this problem is fixed if the 5th player
withdraws and Triple-Ouster lets him -- such that withdrawal
improperly affects the scores of other players, and his own score is
not altered not based on anything he did).

WITHRAWAL -- GENERALLY

Under the standard rules, a withdrawn player merely leaves his
opponents as they stand, taking with him the vp he brought to the
table. He neither ousts nor is ousted. However, as discussed in the
above examples, because of the VEKN's distortions, the withdrawal has
the effect of altering the relative scores of remaining players, and
even granting a game win to one who would not have one -- an effect
certainly never intended by Richard Garfield.

WITHDRAWAL -- OLD VEKN RULES -- COOPERATIVE WITHDRAWAL TO MAXIMIZE VPS

Withdrawal is merely a mechanism for permitting the game to end when
deadlock occurs. It's conditions -- difficult to meet -- are merely
designed to apply where players are likely to be truly deadlocked and
incapable of hurting eachother (eg. -- all minions in torpor with no
blood and no-one has the edge). Otherwise, Garfield would prefer that
the players continue to battle until someone eats or gets eaten.
Some players seem to think that the 1 vp award for withdrawal is a
rewards for accomplishing a technically very difficult task. This is
wrong. Garfield simply wants the (typically) last 2 players to duke
it out in a all or nothing battle for the last 2 vps in the pot. Only
when this seems impossible is he reluctantly willing to permit them to
split those last 2 points, and take one apiece (each walking away with
the vp they brought to the table).

Needless to say, neither Garfield nor the VEKN never intended mass
cooperative withdrawal as a vp maximizing strategy in tournaments. It
was the distortions of the VEKN vp allocation system that made this
possible. Players merely realized that, if deadlocked, some deadlocks
were more profitable than others -- that they could sieze the reward
for "ending the game" without actually doing anything to get the
better of their opponents.

WITHDRAWAL -- NEW VEKN RULES

The VEKN "fixed" this problem by reducing the VP award for successful
withdrawal. This means that, for the first time, the scoring system
for COMPLETED games was altered.

Now, if a 2 remaining deadlocked players are (for example) tied for 1
vp, neither can withdraw without granting his enemy more than he gains
for himself. This would be a distortion in any event, but in this
particular instance the effect is enormous. Neither can withdraw
without granting the other the game win. This is huge. Under the
original rules, when one of two deadlocked and tied players withdraws,
and the other lets him, they remain tied and deadlocked.

Withdrawal is no longer a device for acknowledging deadlock, but for
breaking it. Moreover, the advantage of withdrawal goes to one's
enemy. Hence, withdrawal serves only two functions: 1) a defensive
device to prevent opponents from ousting you; and 2) a method for
colluders to grant victories to their buddies or to grant victories to
opponents pursuant to some secret coin-toss deal.

Note that the former defensive purpose, while not absolutely and
strictly impossible under Garfield's rules, were what his stringent
withdrawal conditions were generally aimed at preventing. Defensive
use of withdrawal is permitted by Garfield's rules, but is not (I
think) the purpose the withdrawal rule was designed for. If a player
needs to withdraw to avoid being ousted, I suspect Garfield would
prefer to let him be ousted.

The second purpose, of course, is entirely illegitimate.

In short, the VEKN might as well ban withdrawal -- leaving "time out"
and mutually agreed draws as the only methods by which deadlocks are
acknowledged.

So you see, I have written a whole bloody essay for you. Plenty of
"distortions" for you. I'm sure you have various reasons for not
thinking they "count" in your book, or have various reasons for not
caring about them. I cannot dictate how another person weighs
evidence nor can I tell you what should or should not matter to you.
But to charge that I have offered no reason or justification for my
views, and to therefore engage in unfriendly speculation as to my real
motives, is, I think, unreasonable.

----------------------

Incidentally, if I thought we still needed to incentivize risk taking
for VPs, I would propose use the following method (which I think is
less of a distortion -- have not given it alot of thought yet):

Each player starts the game with 0 vp. He gains a vp each time he
ousts,and loses one if he is ousted. Negative numbers are ignored,
so, until he scores an oust, each player has nothing to lose. Once
the player has a game win, the lure of a game win takes over as
incentive for risk taking. (Once a player has two game wins, no
futher risk taking incentives are offered him -- it is now up to the
remaining players -- who have nothing to lose and everything to gain
-- to knock him off his throne.)

This offers risk-taking incentives early in the game -- when the
player has nothing to lose -- rather than towards the end, when it is
often too late.

This results in a score similar to a "pure ante" system (resembling
the paradigm of the standard rules for completed games) except that
all results are reduced by one. This naturally necessitates a
revision of the "game win" requirements, as follows:

2 victory points (at game end or time out) are required for a game
win. 1 victory point will suffice, however, in a finished game, if no
other player has 1 victory point.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
<nys...@cs.com> wrote in message
news:1191791463....@o3g2000hsb.googlegroups.com...

> If one expects gripings from unhappy losers even in a well functioning
> system, how can such gripings prove that time outs are a serious
> problem?

I don't think you can prove anything about time outs. There's too
much interaction between players to judge who 'caused' a time out or
what effect a given play or decision had towards causing a time out (or
not). Likewise, there's also too much speculation about what a deck is
intended to do vs. what it actually does when hampered by deck ordering
issues and metagame issues in a given game. Nonetheless, failure
to prove a problem is not the same thing as a problem not existing.
It's not necessary to wave one's hand over deckbuilding and slow play
just because it's difficult to prove who caused what. That's why
the existing system's solution is ideal: apply the same penalty to
all players involved in the game. It's the most you can do but you can
do that and it helps, convoluted and convenient theories around 'causing
frustration' notwithstanding.

> Frederick Scott wrote:
>> People don't make deals to manufacture victory points in tournaments.
>
> They did. Most famous were the cooperative withdrawal deals in the
> earlier VEKN rules -- directly motivated by the failure to conserve
> victory points, and the motive to maximize the table's vps through
> cooperation.

OK, agreed, they did in the past. I don't think it was that bad a
thing but since it made players marginally more successful for
recognizing on upcoming timeout and conspiring to generate 1/2 a
victory point for doing nothing laudable, a positive change was made
to deny that tactic. Now, they don't.

> By "fixing" this problem, the VEKN caused, for the first
> time, a distortion of the victory conditions as applied to completed
> games.

More semantics. Define something you don't like as a 'distortion' -
or whatever negative terminology you think you can get away with -
and hope the negativity will stick and people will agree with your
that it's a bad thing based on the label you want to slap on it.

Oh, wait! Now I'm "calling you a liar", using that same thought process.

>> They can't.
>
> They still can (even if illegal).

Right. What I said: they can't.

> Two deadlocked players can agree to
> toss a coin or roll a dice to see which of them will withdraw and
> surrender a game win to the other -- and unlike a similar agreement to
> forfeiture, this does have any vp cost to the loser of the dice
> role.

They better do the randomization part in the bathroom. And no one better
be hanging around watching the loser play out his position who would
question whether that player is truly playing to win.

And, by the same token, there are lots of ways to cheat through collusion.
It's not an argument to change the scoring system.

>> There's no reason for them to.
>
> Players collude for all kinds of reasons. Colluders are the players
> with the most power to end games. Colluders, therefore, gain the most
> benefit from any game-ending incentives.

I don't see the point to making a wholly inadequate stab at fixing
collusion by changing a scoring system to function in a way that makes
it less capable of addressing a real problem I care about. For all
practical purposes, people can't manufacture victory points.

I'll leave the question on the table of whether your motives are geared
toward facilitating a more sympathetic environment for slower decks
vs....er...whatever other problem or problems you claim to be solving
which never make any coherent sense. It's true, I can't read your mind
and it's possible that you're quite serious about the 'distortion'
thing and/or the 'frustration' thing and whatever else. But it doesn't
matter to me. It always seems to come down to creating an easier road
to the finals for the type of play I'd like to see less of - if anything -
so I'm going to continue to point out its lack of positive qualities
to people.

>> >> And why should we care about this, in practical terms?
>> >
>> > Since you apparently don't care, why bother me with such questions?
>>
>> Ah, but I _do_ care. That's the problem. I don't believe you do.
>
> Well, being called a liar isn't exactly amusing for me, now is it --
> especially after all the effort I have put into defending my
> position.

Notice that no one claim that you lied. I was simply stating my
belief. Equating it to lying is a matter of assuming certain questionable
rhetorical constructions - for instance, what constitutes "caring" about a
thing? What exactly was I claiming you didn't care about vs. what is it
that you believe you do care about? Hint: they are likely not the same
things when explored and that was precisely my point at the time. The
upshot is that you have this awfully annoying rhetorical mannerism of
claiming that you're being insulting when your opponent is simply pointing
out that he doesn't agree with your assessment of a given situation. That's
about all I want to say about this bit. If you want to act insulted by how
I give my opinion, that's your choice. Suffice it to say, I don't agree.

> Fine -- I will give you some distortions, most of which I have alluded
> to elsewhere in thie thread. Note that I am aware that you have
> already dismissed my examples for reasons of your own. I am aware,
> that you may not accept my underlying ideas as to the intent behind
> the original rules. You may not accept my view that Garfield's intent
> in rewarding withdrawal and last man standing was simply to reward
> survival (keep a victory point for not being ousted) and that the
> reason he grants this award at the end of the game or upon withdrawal
> is because that is the point at which it can be determined that the
> player will not be ousted. Nonetheless, those are my views and
> underlying assumption. With that in mind, the scoring paradigm is as
> follows:

Having read through what followed, I find it to be more of the same.
Essentially, it contains a lot values and assumptions with which I
don't agree. Your estimate of what is "intended" by Garfield and
"not intended" is convenient but never mind that. As I pointed out
near the beginning of this thread and once or twice since then, I
question why we should care about that. The original game rules were
created long ago before anyone had any ideas what issues might crop
up and cause problems with the experience of much play under our
belts. Further more, the tournament game _is_ a completely different
game than the non-tournament game and, while it would be nice if
the two were as similar as possible, that's ultimately a lower
priority goal than other things. For instance, the scoring rules
should encourage play that doesn't arbitrarily rob other players of
their chance at a game win based on which opponents they draw in a
given round.

I don't know that there's much more to say about all this. As long
as you continue to assert those values that were part and parcel to
your analysis, I will continue to assert that those values are
irrelevant to what players as a group generally want and, hence,
so is the analysis. This is, of course, a common and arguably
controversial assumption on my part: "The masses agree with me."
It may be false; perhaps people _do_ care a great deal that the game
should faithfully and closely reflect the original intention of
Garfield. Perhaps they would also agree that you've pretty much
defined that intention accurately in your supporting arguments.
This latter point is arguable but moot, IMO. The former would
surprise me a great deal.

Fred

Peter D Bakija wrote:
> In article <1191117326....@19g2000hsx.googlegroups.com>,
> nys...@cs.com wrote:
>
> > I did a bit of searching, and all I could find recently was some
> > posts about FINALISTS who seem willing to permit the final round
> > to go to time because they don't need a "game win" to win the
> > tournament. But this can hardly be what you had in mind.
>
> Why can that hardly be what I had in mind?

Apparently it *was* what you had in mind. But I already explained why
I thought otherwise, so why ask?

My proposal will not effect those factors which cause finals tables to
go to time. Finals players are worried about how will they do
relative to other players at the table. They are worried about
whether they come in first, second, third, fourth or fifth. They are
not worried about the number of vps they get, except as a means to
this end.

A victory point has no inherent value. You cannot take it to the
store after the game and buy two cups of coffee instead of one. It is
a means to an end. In casual games, and in final rounds, victory
points are merely a step in the process of determining who wins, and,
failing that, who comes in second, etc. In finals, a player does not
care whether he comes in first with 1.5 vp or with 2 vp, so long as he
comes in first. This is the fundamental problem in final rounds that
has been causing such a hullaballoo.

Only in preliminary rounds did (does?) the VEKN vp allocution system
marginally incentivize risk, by giving survivors of finished games a
tournament ranking edge over those with an equal number of ousts in
unfinished games. With the shift to the game win system, the focus is
now on gaining game wins, and it is unlikely that such incentives have
any further potential to affect player behavior.

> > As I am sure you realize --
> > my proposed system has no affect on such dynamics whatsoever, for
> > better or worse.
>
> Your proposed system gives 1VP for survival. This encourages folks
> to try a lot harder to not die as opposed to oust their prey,
> which has an effect on the whole dynamic.

I have already explained, in detail, why I think it does not do so.
You snipped my arguments without response.

I have also since posted an alternative risk incentivation proposal.

> Games going to time hurts folks 'cause no one actually wins the
> game. If folks want someone to win the game, they should try
> harder to oust their prey. Giving folks more incentive to wall up
> and *not* try and oust their prey, isn't going to improve this
> dynamic.

Moot, until you address my arguments regarding why I do not believe my
proposal would have such an effect.

> > First of all, a single oust IS worth the same as survival. The
> > rules (which are applied more or less intact in completed games
> > even in tournaments) say so. If you don't like that, you can
> > advocate that the rules be changed.
>
> I don't need to advocate that the rules be changed--as the rules
> stand, you get .5VP for surviving.

Not if the game is completed, you don't. Under the standard rules,
every time a player is not ousted at the end of the game, he gets 1
vp. If you think "merely surviving" should not be rewarded with a
whole, why not be consistent and change the standard rules. A ousts
B, C, and D, then withdraws, leaving E as last man standing. Why
should E get a whole victory point under your value system. He has
done nothing the whole game ... except survive.

The standard rules do not say how to end a game prematurely or how to
score a completed game. The only way to legally end a game
prematurely is collusive withdrawal (easily done if everyone agrees)
which results in 1 vp for everyone.

> If you are the last person at the table, you
> get a full VP for survival, as being the last guy at the table is
> a considerably more significant event that simply surviving till
> time runs out.

Not so, as the above example demonstrates. Being last man standing is
a significant achievement only because it usually means the player has
scored alot of ousts. But ousts are rewarded adequately and
separately.

Last man standing is a survival award, just like withdrawal is a
survival award. Both awards get awarded at the point in the game
where it is determined the player will not be ousted. The standard
rules could be restated as follows: every player brings a vp to the
table with him; gains a point every time he ousts; loses a point if he
gets ousted. Except for the fact that the standard rules do not tell
us how to score unfinished games, the standard rules always follow
this pattern.

> Which is why you get 1VP for being last guy at the table and only
> .5VP for not being ousted when time runs out.

I suspect that this is actually an attempt by the VEKN to incentivize
risk. However, its ability to do so is virtually non-existent now
that the Game Win system is in effect.

> > Irrelevant, since my proposed system does not remove the
> > incentive to oust your prey. Two ousts are still required for a
> > game win (ignoring rare exceptions).
>
> Giving 1VP for still being at the table when time runs out removes
> incentive to oust your prey in any remotely risky situation, [...]

Why? What do you want the victory point for? If you want to get into
the finals, remember (1) a victory point is not a game win; and (2)
more other players will be getting extra vps as well (including many
who scored more ousts than you).

> as defense
> (i.e. walling up and covering your head) is generally less risky
> than offense (going all out to oust your prey even if it means you
> might fail and get ousted). If the reward in a difficult situation
> is 1VP for walling up and covering your head instead of .5VP, you
> have incentive to wall up and cover your head rather than lunging
> for the risky oust. Anything that disincentives folks going for
> the risky oust is bad.

Problem is, you don't actually mean what you say ... as you are about
to admit.

> > If you really mean what you say, perhaps you think the game
> > would be even better if the players received NO points for
> > surviving in timed out games.
>
> I'd be ok with that. Except that, as you note, it makes folks
> arbitrary and reckless. Which is why the current system is
> reasonable--you have more incentive to try and go forward than to
> simply survive, but more incentive to survive than to get ousted.

First you say that anything that does X is bad, then you say it is
merely a matter of achieving the right balance. Well, I believe my
proposal achieves the right balance, ... and to those who are
doubtful, I have offered a second proposal.

> > Please stop pretending you didn't understand me. Please stop
> > pretending I am trying to eliminate the need for ousting.
>
> It is called "rhetorical device", not "pretending".

Why can't it be both? Making a reasonable attempt to acknowledge and
understand your opponent helps things civil and the discussion
constructive. But if words are merely weapons ....

> > Victory points should be awarded based on one's success in
> > besting other players at your table.
>
> Sure. Simply staying alive is not success in besting other players
> at the table.

Neither is withdrawal. Neither is last man standing. Success in
besting other players at the table is measured by ousting, and only by
ousting.

On average, last man standing is more successful than ousting than
other players are. But his level of success is always adequately
measured by counting the number of ousts he achieves.

> Which is why you get .5VP for still being alive when time
> runs out, rather than 1VP.

That can't be why, for the obvious reason stated above.

> As more often than not, being alive when time
> runs out has nothing at all to do with ones actual in game
> position--you could easily be at 1 pool, next to go, and sitting
> in front of an Anarch Revolt without the Edge when time runs out
> during your predator's turn.

Or one could be about to oust one's last enemy and gain 2 vps ... 1 vp
for survival always fairly averages the prospects.

> You survive, sure, but only by arbitrary time limit, not by virtue
> of game play.

Where it is imposed, the arbitrary time limit is part of the game --
ergo you survive by game play. And, of course, it is just as likely
that the arbitrary time limit prevented you from getting more than you
otherwise have gotten.

If two players remain at a table, there is a 50-50 chance that -- but
for the "arbitrary time limit" (or but for withdrawal) -- each will
oust the other. A 50-50 chance of a 2 vp is worth 1 vp.

A simliar (but more complex) calculus could be done for 3, 4, or 5
players remaining at a table. But it will always amount to survival
being worth 1 vp.

> Consequently, the general consensus is that .5VP for
> survivial at time is a reasonable compromise.
>
> > I'm sorry, but that's pretty much what one SHOULD do if one is
> > in a bad position.
>
> See, clearly you do think this, [...]

Yes, in the sense that, under the VEKN rules one SHOULD work to
maximize victory points, when one has no hope of a game win (yes, even
for a half vp). No, to the extent you are trying to pretend I meant
something else, and am trying to de-incentivize risk. I made it clear
enough, in context, that I was NOT talking about incentivizing risk;
and then proceeded to discuss incentivizing risk.

> [...] as your proposal encourages this.

I have argued that it does not, if you mean that my proposal de-
incentivizes risk taking. You have not responded, except to take my
words out of context and try to pretend they meant something other
than that which I clearly intended.

> Which
> I don't believe is actually a good idea. To reward folks for not
> trying to oust their prey. The tournament rules need to reward
> folks for trying to oust their prey over simply surviving.
> Giving .5VP for surviving is a reasonable compromise.

See my second proposal, which incentivizes risk-taking far more
effectively than the current VEKN rules, and also gives some
perspective as why the VEKN rules cannot do so effectively with the
Game Win rules in effect.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
<nys...@cs.com> wrote in message
news:1192984616.5...@q3g2000prf.googlegroups.com...

> Peter D Bakija wrote:
>> I don't need to advocate that the rules be changed--as the rules
>> stand, you get .5VP for surviving.
>
> Not if the game is completed, you don't. Under the standard rules,
> every time a player is not ousted at the end of the game, he gets 1
> vp. If you think "merely surviving" should not be rewarded with a
> whole, why not be consistent and change the standard rules.

Because there's a huge _difference_ in the type of games defined by
the standard rules and the tournament rules, which is what you never
seem to get through your head. Standard rules are the rules played
in games for which it is assumed need never time out. The possibility
of the time out is the thing which makes a lot more difference than
you give it credit for and which makes the distinction important.

> A ousts
> B, C, and D, then withdraws, leaving E as last man standing. Why
> should E get a whole victory point under your value system. He has
> done nothing the whole game ... except survive.

He's done something a survivor-to-timeout has not: held a position
capable of convincing A that he was better off withdrawing at a .5 VP
profit than staying in the game. Why did A bother to withdraw? If
A merely survived to time, he'd get the same payoff and stop E from
getting the extra half .5 VP. A must have had a reason for withdrawing.
That reason is significant.

Surviving to time is certainly less hard than being last man standing
and it is certainly appropriate to view it as being reasonable to
reward it accordingly. And this is the distinction that clearly
divides you and I about your second proposal. You seem to think some
form of rewarding ousts incentizes the end of the game. Bullshit. To
do so fails to recognize the game-lengthening aspects of incentizing
ousts: namely, that players see the need to survive to get the ousts in
order to collect on the incentive. There is little particular
additional incentive to risk one's survival in order to get an ousts,
except perhaps near the end of the game when it often won't matter.

If you want to incentize ending the game effectively, you do this by
incentizing the end of the game - nothing more, nothing less. And the
incentive for ending in the game is *EXACTLY* that .5 VP for being last
man standing. This is my problem with your proposals: you keep
demanding the one true game-resolving incentive be taken away.

> Last man standing is a survival award, just like withdrawal is a
> survival award. Both awards get awarded at the point in the game
> where it is determined the player will not be ousted. The standard
> rules could be restated as follows: every player brings a vp to the
> table with him; gains a point every time he ousts; loses a point if he
> gets ousted. Except for the fact that the standard rules do not tell
> us how to score unfinished games, the standard rules always follow
> this pattern.

The standard rules can be restated that way only if time outs are not
taken into consideration, which the standard rules never needed to.
You seem to think this way of reasoning is unassailable but it's not.
Just because that reasoning works in the absense of the one particular
scenario Richard Garfield didn't need to cover doesn't mean it must
therefore be extended ad naseum each time a new scenario - such as the
need to adjudicate a time out result that crops up in time-limited
tournaments - crops up. It doesn't work right for time outs so screw
it.

The problem here boils down to an overly narrow way of viewing how time
outs change the nature of Jyhad. Equating the challenge of survival-to-
time with that of last-man-standing is a fundamental error.

>> You survive, sure, but only by arbitrary time limit, not by virtue
>> of game play.
>
> Where it is imposed, the arbitrary time limit is part of the game --
> ergo you survive by game play. And, of course, it is just as likely
> that the arbitrary time limit prevented you from getting more than you
> otherwise have gotten.

Maybe, but to reward it equally with to last-man-standing is to encourage
undesirable, problematic strategies and tactics. Of course it has to be
part of the game. But it doesn't need to rewarded in any particular way
as a matter of form. Whatever choice is found to work best in practice
is fine.

Fred

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
In article <1192984616.5...@q3g2000prf.googlegroups.com>,

nys...@cs.com wrote:
> Apparently it *was* what you had in mind. But I already explained why
> I thought otherwise, so why ask?

I posted this, like, 2 weeks ago. Why are you responding to it now? I
mean, like, it isn't a problem. But weird.

> Not if the game is completed, you don't.

That is because if the game is completed, and you are the only survivor
(as games generally can't be completed with more than 1 survivor), you
accomplished more than simply not being ousted when time runs out--you
get .5VP for simply not being ousted when time runs out, as it isn't
really much of an accomplishment. Being the last person left at the
table is takes much more work (you had to oust at least 1 other player
to be the last person standing--to still be alive when time runs out,
you have to simply have been in a game that took longer to oust you than
you had time to be ousted in, and this often has nothing at all to do
with your actual game play, deck, or position). Consequently, it makes
perfect sense to me that a person who is the last person at the table
gets 1VP, where someone who is simply not ousted when time runs out gets
only .5VP.

> Under the standard rules,
> every time a player is not ousted at the end of the game, he gets 1
> vp.

You are portraying "every time a player is not ousted" in a standard
game as being the same as someone still being alive when time runs out
in a tournament game. When they are not actually the same thing. Being
not ousted in a standard game means that you are the last person at the
table. Which means you killed someone to get there. Which means you did
something proactive and accomplished something. In a tournament game,
being still alive when time runs out means nothing of the sort. It just
means that you had at least 1 pool when time ran out. Comparing the two
is not really viable

> If you think "merely surviving" should not be rewarded with a
> whole, why not be consistent and change the standard rules.

The standard rules don't include a time limit, so changing the standard
rules based on the tournament rules that include a time limit is
pointless. In a standard game, surviving to the end of the game means
you are the last person at the table. And you ousted someone to get
there. This is, in the context of the game, an accomplishment that is
worth incentivizing and rewarding. Thus, a full VP. Conversely, in
tournament play, being alive when time runs out is certainly some sort
of accomplishment (although how big of an accomplishment is certainly up
to debate based on a given game), so it gets some sort of reward (.5
VP), but not the same reward as being the last person left at the table.
Which strikes me as totally logical.

> A ousts
> B, C, and D, then withdraws, leaving E as last man standing. Why
> should E get a whole victory point under your value system. He has
> done nothing the whole game ... except survive.

This is a ridiculously trumped up example. Why is player A withdrawing
after ousting 3 people? If it is 'cause player E is too tough to oust?
Well, then E has done something other than just survive--he has foiled
the clearly superior player A. If it is for any reason other than this,
the situation is falling outside of the realm of the game rules, as it
is clearly for irrational (or in a tournament, illegal) reasons.

> The standard rules do not say how to end a game prematurely or how to
> score a completed game.

'Cause the standard rules assume there is no time limit. The tournament
rules have a time limit. This is a significant difference, that leads to
different rules.

> The only way to legally end a game
> prematurely is collusive withdrawal (easily done if everyone agrees)
> which results in 1 vp for everyone.

Why is this happening in a non tournament game? And why does anyone
care? You are inventing examples that have no place in reality and
trying to use them to support your argument.

> Why? What do you want the victory point for? If you want to get into
> the finals, remember (1) a victory point is not a game win; and (2)
> more other players will be getting extra vps as well (including many
> who scored more ousts than you).

A single victory point is worth more in tournament scoring than zero
victory points. You want the victory point as it increases your standing.

> Where it is imposed, the arbitrary time limit is part of the game --
> ergo you survive by game play. And, of course, it is just as likely
> that the arbitrary time limit prevented you from getting more than you
> otherwise have gotten.

Sure. As it is likely to be all sorts of things, it makes sense to split
the difference. And get you .5VP. You could be about to oust someone
when time runs out. You could also be at 1 pool and have zero minions
when time runs out. Either is just as likely. So you average things out.
.5VP.

> I have argued that it does not, if you mean that my proposal de-
> incentivizes risk taking. You have not responded, except to take my
> words out of context and try to pretend they meant something other
> than that which I clearly intended.

I have explained why I think your proposal de-incentivizes risk taking.
And will do so again--if you get a full VP for simply surviving, if you
are in a questionable position, you have all the incentive in the world
to not try for the 1VP oust and and instead wall up and slow down the
game. With .5VP for simply surviving, you have more incentive to take a
risk for the oust if there is a chance for it.

Peter D Bakija

> Because there's a huge _difference_ in the type of games defined by
> the standard rules and the tournament rules, which is what you
> never seem to get through your head.

I have discussed and analysed those differences at length. You, on
the other hand, have repeatedly said you don't care about those
differences. All you offer now is conclusory statements and hot air.

> Standard rules are the rules played
> in games for which it is assumed need never time out. The
> possibility of the time out is the thing which makes a lot more
> difference than you give it credit for and which makes the
> distinction important.

Until you elaborate with some analysis, this is merely hot air.

> > A ousts
> > B, C, and D, then withdraws, leaving E as last man standing. Why
> > should E get a whole victory point under your value system. He
> > has done nothing the whole game ... except survive.
>
> He's done something a survivor-to-timeout has not: held a position
> capable of convincing A that he was better off withdrawing at a .5
> VP profit than staying in the game.

He's done the exact same thing the survivor til time out has done ...
survived til the end of the game. The distinction you make is based
on invented facts, not part of the scenario described.

> Why did A bother to withdraw?

Who cares? No-doubt he was out of cards. Perhaps he suspected
(perhaps falsely) that his opponent would be able to oust him within
the time limit. In any event, he prevented his predator from ousting
him; but failed to oust his prey. Nobody wins (until and unless other
ousts are considered). That's what withdrawal means.

> If A merely survived to time, he'd get the same payoff and stop E
> from getting the extra half .5 VP. A must have had a reason for
> withdrawing. That reason is significant.

To you, maybe. Not to me. Certainly not to the designer of the
standard rules. Under the standard rules, if two players remaining in
the game are tied for 1 vp, and one withdraws, the one who convinced
the other to withdraw does not get extra credit for forcing his
opponent to withdraw. After the withdrawal, they remain tied, exactly
as they were before.

Under the standard rules, the withdrawal of ones opponent is not a
second-class victory. It is not a poor-man's oust. It is not a
victory at all.

> Surviving to time is certainly less hard than being last man
> standing and it is certainly appropriate to view it as being
> reasonable to reward it accordingly.

Only because being last man standing normally requires ousting other
players, particularly one's prey. That is the only reason why it is
harder.

> And this is the distinction that clearly
> divides you and I about your second proposal. You seem to think
> some form of rewarding ousts incentizes the end of the game.

Yup. You read me right for once.

> Bullshit. To
> do so fails to recognize the game-lengthening aspects of
> incentizing ousts: namely, that players see the need to survive to
> get the ousts in order to collect on the incentive.

I have not failed to recognize anything.

> There is little particular
> additional incentive to risk one's survival in order to get an
> ousts, except perhaps near the end of the game when it often won't
> matter.

Evidently, you do not understand the proposal. My proposal
incentivises risk. I have offered analysis to support this, which I
need not repeat. All you offer is grand conclusory declarations.

> If you want to incentize ending the game effectively, you do this
> by incentizing the end of the game - nothing more, nothing less.

I think that is totally idiotic, and I think you are making a complete
ass of yourself by repeating it. Players cannot waive a magic wand
and end the game.

Players can do 4 things to end the game:

1. Withdraw
2. Oust cross-table
3. Oust their prey
4. Oust themselves

To which their could be added a 5th (which, as far as the incentive is
concerned, is really a variant of "oust your prey"):

5. Incentivize risk -- risk getting ousted in the course of
desperately trying to oust prey.

My proposal promotes game ending by rewarding ousting (#3) or by
rewarding #5 (risk taking). (It also rewards withdrawal more than the
current proposal, though it does not do this in order to risk
incentivize).

We have already agreed that #4 should not be directly incentivized.
As for #2, we know Garfield sought to minimize that by the predator
prey relationship, and most folks seem to think that is a dynamic
worth preserving. That leaves the method I have adopted -- ousting
prey (together with promiting risk taking for the sake of ousting
prey).

> And the
> incentive for ending in the game is *EXACTLY* that .5 VP for being
> last man standing. This is my problem with your proposals: you
> keep demanding the one true game-resolving incentive be taken away.

As you previously acknowledged, the game win system has been far more
effective at incentivizing risk. It does so not by rewarding last man
standing, but by rewarding the achievement of (normally) two ousts.
My alternate proposal does the same. It does not (idiotially,
uselessly, stupidly) offer measley half-vp bribes to decks that have
already acheived a game win.

> > Last man standing is a survival award, just like withdrawal is a
> > survival award. Both awards get awarded at the point in the game
> > where it is determined the player will not be ousted. The
> > standard rules could be restated as follows: every player
> > brings a vp to the table with him; gains a point every time he
> > ousts; loses a point if he gets ousted. Except for the fact
> > that the standard rules do not tell us how to score unfinished
> > games, the standard rules always follow this pattern.
>
> The standard rules can be restated that way only if time outs are

> not taken into consideration, [...]

That's exactly what I said ... except I omitted the word "only". I do
not assume, as you do, that Garfield would have made an exception had
he taken time outs into consideration.

> [...] which the standard rules never needed to.

Hmmm?

> You seem to think this way of reasoning is unassailable but it's
> not.

Clearly not, since you are assailing it. You have proven that my
proposal is assailable by people who lack understanding.

> Just because that reasoning works in the absense of the one
> particular scenario Richard Garfield didn't need to cover doesn't
> mean it must therefore be extended ad naseum each time a new
> scenario - such as the need to adjudicate a time out result that
> crops up in time-limited tournaments - crops up.

I have offered extensive analysis supporting my view that it should be
extended to time out. I have extensively shown the distortions that
result from doing otherwise. Your response has been simply "I don't
care." So what the hell are you going on about now?

> It doesn't work right for time outs so screw it.

Oh, I believe it does work for time outs ... quite well.

> The problem here boils down to an overly narrow way of viewing how
> time outs change the nature of Jyhad. Equating the challenge of

> survival-to-time with that of last-man-standing is a fundamental
> error.

I see no error.

> >> You survive, sure, but only by arbitrary time limit, not by virtue
> >> of game play.
> >
> > Where it is imposed, the arbitrary time limit is part of the
> > game -- ergo you survive by game play. And, of course, it is
> > just as likely that the arbitrary time limit prevented you from
> > getting more than you otherwise have gotten.
>
> Maybe, but to reward it equally with to last-man-standing is to
> encourage undesirable, problematic strategies and tactics.

How? It is about time you supported your nonsense with some examples
and analysis. Provide an coherent example of a situation where the
current system incentivizes risk taking, but where my proposals do
not.

> Of course it has to be
> part of the game. But it doesn't need to rewarded in any
> particular way as a matter of form. Whatever choice is found to
> work best in practice is fine.

My proposal has never been tried in practice. So I guess this is what
you think supports your conclusory statements.

Messages.Body:

Bullshit. Obviously, I do care about the difference, you misinterpretations
of anything I've said in the past not withstanding. You are throwing
rhetorical furniture in the way of a pursuer hot on your heels, here.

The problem with your claims is exactly what you just said: all of your
rhetoric about it is based on long-winded analysis, not clear and succinct
reasoning. I've examined your analysis and found no new ground in any
of it - just the same errors repeated over and over in lots of boring
little paragraphs. I could drag out your analysis and point these out
but you'll forgive me if I assume that I'll just get the same circular
answers you've repeatedly offered in the past, perhaps in yet _longer_
form, who knows?

What I find very interesting is that whenever I attempt to summarize
these long, point-by-point posts of yours so that people who don't care
to find them and wade through them, you angrily accuse me of putting
words in your mouth. Yet at the same time, you refuse to offer your
*OWN* position about these issues in any succinct way. My conclusion
is that you actually don't want people to know what it is: to do so would
put its weakness on display for the masses. So every response is a wave
of a hand, pointing people back to those long-winded and now difficult-to-
find month old posts.

>> Standard rules are the rules played
>> in games for which it is assumed need never time out. The
>> possibility of the time out is the thing which makes a lot more
>> difference than you give it credit for and which makes the
>> distinction important.

...

>> > A ousts
>> > B, C, and D, then withdraws, leaving E as last man standing. Why
>> > should E get a whole victory point under your value system. He
>> > has done nothing the whole game ... except survive.
>>
>> He's done something a survivor-to-timeout has not: held a position
>> capable of convincing A that he was better off withdrawing at a .5
>> VP profit than staying in the game.
>
> He's done the exact same thing the survivor til time out has done ...
> survived til the end of the game. The distinction you make is based
> on invented facts, not part of the scenario described.

"Invented facts"?!? YOU constructed the scenario. YOU invented player
A who chose to withdraw, NOT ME!!!

>> Why did A bother to withdraw?
>
> Who cares?

I care! Everybody should care! Show me the reason A withdrew and I'll
show you the reason it's appropriate to reward E with an extra .5 VP,
where it wouldn't be if E merely survived to time.

>No-doubt he was out of cards.

Fine. Then he lost. Or at least, he lost his .5 VP in comparison to
Player E. People lose when they run out of resources and their opponents
thereby win. This is totally appropriate.

Don't forget, it's very hard to withdraw in such a situation. In most
cases, if A runs out of cards, he doesn't withdraw. He'd usually get
ousted by any competant player E. If he can manage to withdraw, then
he gets an extra .5 VP he normally wouldn't have had.

> Perhaps he suspected
> (perhaps falsely) that his opponent would be able to oust him within
> the time limit.

Then he screwed up and Player E won for managing to look formidable.
Sometimes, looking more formidable than your are is rewardable. Ask a
rush combat player who threatens his crosstable ally into taking
a favorable action for him even when he doesn't hold the means to
actually punish his ally in his hand.

> In any event, he prevented his predator from ousting
> him; but failed to oust his prey. Nobody wins (until and unless other
> ousts are considered). That's what withdrawal means.

No, that is not "what withdrawal means". You've conflated two unlike
scenarios and the confusion is driving you to an incorrect conclusion.

>> If A merely survived to time, he'd get the same payoff and stop E
>> from getting the extra half .5 VP. A must have had a reason for
>> withdrawing. That reason is significant.
>
> To you, maybe. Not to me. Certainly not to the designer of the
> standard rules

...who was not covering the issue of time outs when he designed them.
Every time you take that tact, you will get this response. So you
are wasting your breath to take it without presenting some kind of
answer to this. Survival-to-time does not equate to withdrawal.

>> You seem to think
>> some form of rewarding ousts incentizes the end of the game.
>
> Yup. You read me right for once.
>
>> Bullshit. To do so fails to recognize the game-lengthening aspects
>> of incentizing ousts: namely, that players see the need to survive

>> to get the ousts in order to collect on the incentive. There is little

>> particular additional incentive to risk one's survival in order to get
>> an ousts, except perhaps near the end of the game when it often won't
>> matter.
>
> Evidently, you do not understand the proposal. My proposal
> incentivises risk. I have offered analysis to support this, which I
> need not repeat. All you offer is grand conclusory declarations.

The declarations effectively state the dispute. Your "analysis", as
per above, merely tends to hide the weakness in your position.

>> If you want to incentize ending the game effectively, you do this
>> by incentizing the end of the game - nothing more, nothing less.
>

> Players cannot waive a magic wand and end the game.
>
> Players can do 4 things to end the game:
>
> 1. Withdraw
> 2. Oust cross-table
> 3. Oust their prey
> 4. Oust themselves
>
> To which their could be added a 5th (which, as far as the incentive is
> concerned, is really a variant of "oust your prey"):
>
> 5. Incentivize risk -- risk getting ousted in the course of
> desperately trying to oust prey.

Sure. I'm not sure how #5 falls in a different category than
#3 but I'm glad you specifically identified it because it _is_
important. Your pat little list of actions which could be contribute
to the end of the game is an overly narrow, insufficient way of
analyzing the issue of what contributes to ending game before vs.
after a time limit. #5 is exactly the point: HOW one attempts to
oust one's prey is as important to this end as the oust, itself.
In fact, given that usually everybody on the table is attempting to
oust their prey - albeit in different ways - it is actually a lot
more important. So worrying about "incentizing ousts" in order to
resolve games sooner misses the point: ousts are incentized just fine
in the rules as it is. Incentizing taking risks to get ousts is
much more to the point, since the goal of resolving the game is
served either way if risk-taking is encouarged.

> My proposal promotes game ending by rewarding ousting (#3) or by
> rewarding #5 (risk taking).

It actually doesn't reward risk taking nearly as much as you claim.
You take away .8 VP from players who have no ousts instead of .5.
But taking away with one hand, you give back with the other: giving
back the .5 VP from players who have two or more ousts that would
have provided them incentive to resolve the game. And the incentive
isn't really all that big of an incentive anyway except towards the
end of game. The nature of the game is that if you survive, you may
get a chance later in the game to make a much better lunge than you
can make now. And even if you have a lunge you can make now that's
not too bad, you may succeed at getting the oust - and wind up getting
ousted anyway. My conclusion is that the main incentive for making
a lunge provided in your second proposal is towards the end of the
game. So the game may well time out anyway, even if the isolated
extra lunge is taken and even if some of those isolated extra lunges
succeed some of time (I think they won't in most cases). Big deal.

>> And the
>> incentive for ending in the game is *EXACTLY* that .5 VP for being
>> last man standing. This is my problem with your proposals: you
>> keep demanding the one true game-resolving incentive be taken away.
>
> As you previously acknowledged, the game win system has been far more
> effective at incentivizing risk. It does so not by rewarding last man
> standing, but by rewarding the achievement of (normally) two ousts.
> My alternate proposal does the same.

But relative to the existing system, it's not as good.

And there's a reason I like the extra incentive: it deliberately values
last-man-standing victories as superior to two-plus-ousts-and-survive
victories, oust-per-oust. I want that. That incentizes faster less-
risk-of-timeout play in general. If I could, I'd jack the incentive
up some more. It's just that I don't see how to accomplish it without
too much risk of punishing things which were just misfortune (table
in which everyone's prey, by chance, had an effective defense and an
ineffective offense). So I like things as they are, unless someone
shows me a better way to do it.

> It does not (idiotially,
> uselessly, stupidly) offer measley half-vp bribes to decks that have
> already acheived a game win.

The reason is that people who bring decks that risk time outs export
that risk to their faster opponents who had the misfortune to play
against them. This is unfair. This is a point you also refuse to
acknowledge or take into account. You may have your opinion; I think
the reason is very good.

(elided the same repetitious dispute about whether standard rules can
be readily extended to play where time outs need to be scored in the
simplistic manner John claims...)

>> > Where it is imposed, the arbitrary time limit is part of the
>> > game -- ergo you survive by game play. And, of course, it is
>> > just as likely that the arbitrary time limit prevented you from
>> > getting more than you otherwise have gotten.
>>
>> Maybe, but to reward it equally with to last-man-standing is to
>> encourage undesirable, problematic strategies and tactics.
>
> How? It is about time you supported your nonsense with some examples
> and analysis.

Above - the previous paragraph about drawing opponents using slower
developing decks.

> Provide an coherent example of a situation where the
> current system incentivizes risk taking, but where my proposals do
> not.

Simple. Take the example of Tzimisce intercept combat deck. It has
little direct forward means of ousting its prey in the early part of
the game other than intercepting its prey taking undirected actions or
the occasion Eagles Sight it can pull out. It doesn't need such means.
It can stop its predator for ousting it in most cases and usually punish
the predator for even trying by torping the predator's minions in the
resulting combats.

It plays things like Powerbase: Montreal, hunting ground, Palatial Estate,
and blood dolls to build up. It may risk allowing its prey to get some
ousts but in many circumstances, simply stopping enough of its prey's
undirected actions (or, in a lot of case the prey just doesn't bother taking
them) and the Eagle's Sights will stop the prey from getting an ousts.
Anyway, if the table does collapse some, who cares? The Tzimisce deck
usually won't win through a 5-player sweep anyway. But after enough time
has passed, it will bloat up slowly and build up in numbers enough to start
bleeding forward while still having enough defense to be comfortable. Maybe
it's succeeded at Pulsing or maybe the table is now small enough to win with
a Smiling Jack. Or maybe it's just beaten up its prey enough that small
bleeds will do the trick.

I've seen this kind of a deck work just fine. It was weaknesses, of course.
But on balance, it metagames pretty good. The problem with it is that it
slows down the game and risks no-game-win time outs even when it doesn't
win. So it becomes an unfair punishment for other players to wind up stuck
in the same game with it while others get to play against decks that, win
or lose, don't cause that problem.

>> Of course it has to be
>> part of the game. But it doesn't need to rewarded in any
>> particular way as a matter of form. Whatever choice is found to
>> work best in practice is fine.
>
> My proposal has never been tried in practice.

You mistake my meaning. I don't mean "in practice" as in, it has to be
physically used. One can foresee the effect your proposals would have in
practice. I mean "in practice" as in, taking ALL the phenomena observed in
real world play into account. Not just the ones your narrow theories choose
to account for.

Fred
