Peter D Bakija wrote:
> I posted this, like, 2 weeks ago. Why are you responding to it
> now? I mean, like, it isn't a problem. But weird.

People normally respond when they find the time. Why is an
explanation needed?

> > Not if the game is completed, you don't.
>
> That is because if the game is completed, and you are the only
> survivor (as games generally can't be completed with more than 1
> survivor), you accomplished more than simply not being ousted when
> time runs out--

That "more" consists of ousting prey -- normally.

> [...] you

> get .5VP for simply not being ousted when time runs out, as it
> isn't really much of an accomplishment.

If you get a whole vp for being last man standing (and do not oust)
that is not much of an accomplishment either. I never took the
position that last man standing who scores an oust has accomplished
more than a time out player who has not scored an oust. I merely too
the position that a last man standing with one oust should be worth
the same as a time out player with one oust.

I never denied that last man standing will on average have achieved
more ousts than a time out player. But this level of success is
already measured by the number of ousts he gets.

> Being the last person left at the
> table is takes much more work (you had to oust at least 1 other
> player to be the last person standing--to still be alive when time

> runs out, [...]

Usually you do have to oust someone to be last man standing. But that
ousting gets its own reward of one vp per oust. To determine if "last
man standing" is inherently deserving of more than survival til time
out, you have to look at those situations where a time out player and
a last man standing have scored an equal number of ousts.

> [...] you have to simply have been in a game that took longer to

> oust you than you had time to be ousted in, and this often has
> nothing at all to do with your actual game play, deck, or
> position).

You are skewing the assumptions -- assuming that a player who goes to
time -- but for the time limit -- is about to be ousted, rather than
that he is about to oust -- there is an equal chance of either.

> Consequently, it makes
> perfect sense to me that a person who is the last person at the
> table gets 1VP, where someone who is simply not ousted when time
> runs out gets only .5VP.

Not to me ... (except as a risk incentivizing device, now obsolete
with the game win system in place).

> > Under the standard rules,
> > every time a player is not ousted at the end of the game, he
> > gets 1 vp.
>
> You are portraying "every time a player is not ousted" in a
> standard game as being the same as someone still being alive when
> time runs out in a tournament game.

I simply made a true statement about the standard rules. As I have
explicitly acknowledged many times, the standard rules do not address
time outs -- so that is an extension of the pattern on my part.

> When they are not actually the same thing. Being
> not ousted in a standard game means that you are the last person
> at the table.

Either that, or it means successful withdrawal. Both gain 1 vp.

> Which means you killed someone to get there.

If you killed someone to get there, you get a vp for killing someone
to get there -- or more than 1 vp, if you killed more than one to get
there. So that is already accounted for. The 1vp for last man
standing is awarded above and beyond that, and is awarded even if you
did not kill anyone to get there.

> Which means you did
> something proactive and accomplished something.

No. If you did anything proactive (like ousting), and accomplished
anything (like ousting), you have already been rewarded for it. To
the extent that last man standing awards anything beyond that, it
merely awards survival.

You seem to want to pretend that I believe that the last man standing
with one oust should be rewarded the same as a time out player with no
ousts. But that is to argue with a straw man. Clearly, my position
is that the former should get 2 vp and the latter should get 1 vp.

> In a tournament game,
> being still alive when time runs out means nothing of the sort. It
> just means that you had at least 1 pool when time ran out.

Or it could mean your prey had one pool when time ran out. There is
an equal chance of either. Stop skewing the facts in your favor.

> Comparing the two is not really viable

Seems viable to me.

> > If you think "merely surviving" should not be rewarded with a
> > whole, why not be consistent and change the standard rules.
>
> The standard rules don't include a time limit, so changing the
> standard rules based on the tournament rules that include a time
> limit is pointless. In a standard game, surviving to the end of
> the game means you are the last person at the table.

Right.

> And you ousted someone to get there.

If you did, you get an extra vp for ousting. Why are you pretending I
am trying to change that?

> This is, in the context of the game, an accomplishment that is
> worth incentivizing and rewarding.

Are you trying to pretend my proposal does not reward him? It gives
him 1 vp for ousting, plus one for last man standing, for a total of 2
vp. It gives the same to a time-out player if AND ONLY IF he scores
the same number of ousts. A time out player who scores no ousts gets
only 1`vp under my proposal.

> Thus, a full VP. Conversely, in
> tournament play, being alive when time runs out is certainly some
> sort of accomplishment (although how big of an accomplishment is
> certainly up to debate based on a given game), so it gets some
> sort of reward (.5 VP), but not the same reward as being the last
> person left at the table.

> Which strikes me as totally logical.

It does not seem logical to me, because you are guilty of double
counting. You want to reward the the last man standing for scoring
more ousts, but have forgotten that he has already been awarded for
this, to the extent that he has done it.

> > A ousts
> > B, C, and D, then withdraws, leaving E as last man standing. Why
> > should E get a whole victory point under your value system. He has
> > done nothing the whole game ... except survive.
>
> This is a ridiculously trumped up example.

It is an appropriate example. You want to cheat by comparing the last
man standing with 1 oust to the time out player with no ousts, and
argue that the last man standing with one oust is more deserving. Of
course he is! And my proposal gives him more -- it gives him 1 extra
vp for that extra oust that he got.

You want to harp on the time out player with no ousts. But the
appropriate comparison to the time out player with no ousts is the
last man standing with no ousts.

If you want a less "ridiculous trumped up" example, we should compare
the time out player with 3 ousts to the last man standing with 3
ousts. To my mind, they are both equally deserving -- they have
ousted three players, and should both get 4 vp.

The difference lies in the uncertainty. Had the time out game
finished, then our winning player might have gotten ousted (and ended
with 3 vp instead of 4); but it is at least equally likely (at least)
that he would have ousted his prey and ended up with 5. So he splits
the difference and gets 4. Perfectly fair.

> Why is player A withdrawing after ousting 3 people?
> If it is 'cause player E is too tough to oust?

Could be ... after all, Player A did run out of cards. But if player
E was so tough, why did he let A withdraw?

> Well, then E has done something other than just survive--he has
> foiled the clearly superior player A.

You are assuming facts not in evidence. The only way E has foiled A
is to avoid A's attempt to oust him. In other words, E survived until
the end of the game. That is all E managed to accomplish -- not being
ousted.

> If it is for any reason other than this,
> the situation is falling outside of the realm of the game rules,
> as it is clearly for irrational (or in a tournament, illegal)
> reasons.

I think you're getting a bit carried away. There is no reason to
discuss collusion. If you prefer a different example, where A's
motives might be clearer, how about 4 player game: A ousts B, then
ousts C, then withdraws. E (wuss that he is) lets him. A wins 3 vp
to 1 vp standard rules (2.5 vp to 1 vp VEKN rules). Here we see that
A by withdrawing secures himself the game win. His motives are clear
enough. Even if he thought that there was a 95% percent chance that
he would oust E, and an only 5% chance that he would be ousted, then
the decision to withdraw would be rational if he thereby secured for
himself a 100% game win.

> > The standard rules do not say how to end a game prematurely or
> > how to score a completed game.
>
> 'Cause the standard rules assume there is no time limit. The
> tournament rules have a time limit. This is a significant
> difference, that leads to different rules.

More because it does not matter. Casual players wanting to end games
prematurely could (if they wish) arrange collusive withdrawal (just as
tournament players eventually learned to do). But there is no reason
to, because that extra vp has no meaning if it does not come from
besting your opponent and winning the game.

Casual players use common sense. A,B,C,D,E sit at table. A ousts B,
E ousts A. The 3 remaining players go to time, and have to go home to
their wives. They understand perfectly well who was doing best at the
table, who was in first place when time was called. It was E. B is
dead last. A, C, and D are somewhere in the middle, and I would guess
that C and D do not feel that they are doing any worse than A did.
Certainly E knows he is in a better position than A, even though so
far he has the same number of vps.

If that extra had any inherent value to them -- if they could take it
to the store and buy two cups of coffee -- then C, D and E could
easily arrange for a collusive withdrawal, and end the game: A,B,C,D,E
getting 1, 0, 1, 1, 2. This resulf fairly reflects the strength of
their position.

> > The only way to legally end a game
> > prematurely is collusive withdrawal (easily done if everyone
> > agrees) which results in 1 vp for everyone.
>
> Why is this happening in a non tournament game? And why does
> anyone care?

They don't. The example is for theoretical illustration. In casual
games, victory points are merely a means to an end. If they did
matter (if they were part of an economy external to the game, as in
preliminary tournament rounds) then it could easily be done. This
thought exercise shows how many vps they would get in a timed out
game, under the standard rules IF IT MATTERED TO THEM.

> You are inventing examples that have no place in reality and
> trying to use them to support your argument.

Perhaps you don't understand my point.

> > Why? What do you want the victory point for? If you want to
> > get into the finals, remember (1) a victory point is not a game
> > win; and (2) more other players will be getting extra vps as
> > well (including many who scored more ousts than you).
>
> A single victory point is worth more in tournament scoring than
> zero victory points.

So is a half victory point. You need more than that to make the
finals.

> You want the victory point as it increases your standing.

You want more than the victory point, under my proposal, for the same
reasons you want more than the half victory point under the current
system. Alot of players are going to be getting more, so you need
more to be competitive. The idea that players will stop wanting to
oust, because they can get one whole victory point by surviving, is
silly. This is especially so in a 40 player tournament. If you want
to be one of the 5 finalists, you are not going to be satisfied with
an average number of vps and a below-average number of game wins.

> > Where it is imposed, the arbitrary time limit is part of the
> > game -- ergo you survive by game play. And, of course, it is
> > just as likely that the arbitrary time limit prevented you from
> > getting more than you otherwise have gotten.
>
> Sure. As it is likely to be all sorts of things, it makes sense to
> split the difference.

That's exactly what I have done. I did it correctly. You did it
incorrectly.

In a 2-player context, there's 3 ways it can go:

2, 0 (A ousts B)
0, 2 (B ousts A)
1, 1 (simultaneous ousts -- or 1 player withdraws)

Splitting the difference gives one per player.

In the context of 3 remaining players, the possibilities for a
completed game are as follows:

3, 0, 0
0, 3, 0
0, 0, 3
2, 1, 0
2, 0, 1
1, 2, 0
1, 0, 2
0, 2, 1
0, 1, 2
1, 1, 1

Average it all up, and you get one vp per player. (10 vp per column
divided by 10 rows). You could achieve the same result with 4 or 5
player games.

> And get you .5VP.

No. Splitting the difference is 1 vp. You are falsely assuming that
only one vp remains to be earned, and falsely averaging this against
the one vp the player has to lose. In fact, there are at least 2 vp
remaining to be earned.

> You could be about to oust someone
> when time runs out. You could also be at 1 pool and have zero
> minions when time runs out. Either is just as likely. So you
> average things out. .5VP.

If there are 2 players remaining, splitting the difference gets you 1
vp, as shown above. If there are 3 players remaining, splitting the
difference gets you 1 vp, as shown above.

> > I have argued that it does not, if you mean that my proposal de-
> > incentivizes risk taking. You have not responded, except to
> > take my words out of context and try to pretend they meant
> > something other than that which I clearly intended.
>
> I have explained why I think your proposal de-incentivizes risk
> taking. And will do so again--if you get a full VP for simply
> surviving, if you are in a questionable position, you have all the
> incentive in the world to not try for the 1VP oust and and instead
> wall up and slow down the game. With .5VP for simply surviving,
> you have more incentive to take a risk for the oust if there is a
> chance for it.

Okay. Since you won't provide an example, I will.

A ousts B and C; D oust E. Now its E against A. A thinks he has a
chance to oust E, but it is very risky. E thinks he has a chance to
oust A, but it is very risky.

Under current VEKN rules, E will not take the risk of trying to oust
A. He would rather go to time (if he can), and not risk losing the
game win (but if he knows he cannot make it to time, he will want to
oust before he gets ousted). Sure, he will get +1.5 vp for risking
and winning, just as he will lose only 0.5 for losing, but along with
that 0.5 he will also lose the game win -- That vp award is not
relevant when the game win is at stake. E, however, has every reason
to try to oust A, not mainly because of the extra 1.5 vps, but because
of the game win.

Under either of my proposals, the dynamics will be exactly the same --
the players will be focussed on the game win, and ignore the useless
half vp bribe.

Please provide a counterexample, where it would make a difference in
terms of player behavior.

nys...@cs.com wrote:
> People normally respond when they find the time. Why is an

An explanation isn't needed. But still. Weird. But maybe that is just
me. Like, I'll respond to something when it happens, and if I don't? Not
so much go back 2 weeks and readdress it. But ok.

> If you get a whole vp for being last man standing (and do not oust)
> that is not much of an accomplishment either. I never took the
> position that last man standing who scores an oust has accomplished
> more than a time out player who has not scored an oust. I merely too
> the position that a last man standing with one oust should be worth
> the same as a time out player with one oust.

Again, the difference is that being the last man standing at the table
means you have either ousted someone over and above the timeout player,
or forced another player to withdraw (which is often a feat in and of
itself). The position that last man standing with 1 oust should be worth
the same as a timeout player with an oust is clearly the issue that you
are having trouble convincing folks should be an equivelant position. I
don't think they are equivelant positions.

Being alive when the game times out holds no specific accomplishment--as
I note elsewhere, sometimes when you are alive when the game times out,
you are on the verge of a sweep. Just as often, you are in a totally
lost position, and the timeout saves you from inevitable death. The
timeout doesn't make a distinction. It just gives you an average
reward--.5 VP.

> I never denied that last man standing will on average have achieved
> more ousts than a time out player. But this level of success is
> already measured by the number of ousts he gets.

It isn't the number of ousts that gets you the extra .5VP over simply
being alive when time runs out. Being the last man standing is the
result of being in an advantageous position--you either ousted the last
other player *or* you forced them to withdraw (and the vast majority of
the time, you are ousting the last other player). Either of these are
"accomplishments" so much as anything in the game is.

> Usually you do have to oust someone to be last man standing. But that
> ousting gets its own reward of one vp per oust. To determine if "last
> man standing" is inherently deserving of more than survival til time
> out, you have to look at those situations where a time out player and
> a last man standing have scored an equal number of ousts.

Again, timing out is an artificial imposition on the playing field, and
makes no value judgement--you might time out in a great position or time
out in a horrible position. Likely equal likelyhood of either. Thus,
average reward--.5VP.

> You are skewing the assumptions -- assuming that a player who goes to
> time -- but for the time limit -- is about to be ousted, rather than
> that he is about to oust -- there is an equal chance of either.

Exactly. An equal chance of either. Average the reward. .5VP.

> If you killed someone to get there, you get a vp for killing someone
> to get there -- or more than 1 vp, if you killed more than one to get
> there. So that is already accounted for. The 1vp for last man
> standing is awarded above and beyond that, and is awarded even if you
> did not kill anyone to get there.

You can't be the last man standing without either killing someone or
forcing someone to withdraw. You are never going to be in a situation,
other than by virtue of negotiation, where you will be the last man
standing due to someone withdrawing when you can't either stop them or
oust them.

> No. If you did anything proactive (like ousting), and accomplished
> anything (like ousting), you have already been rewarded for it. To
> the extent that last man standing awards anything beyond that, it
> merely awards survival.

No, it awards being the last man standing. Which is, as noted
ad-nauseum, different than being alive when time runs out. Time running
out is, for all intents and purposes, a random effect. The game ends at
some point, and the position you are in when time runs out could just as
well be determined by die roll. Being last man standing comes from being
in an advantageous position and playing well. Being alive when time runs
out could just as likely be the result of random chance as good play.
Thus, split the difference. .5VP.

> You seem to want to pretend that I believe that the last man standing
> with one oust should be rewarded the same as a time out player with no
> ousts. But that is to argue with a straw man. Clearly, my position
> is that the former should get 2 vp and the latter should get 1 vp.

No, I want to pretend that you want to give a player who times out 1VP
instead of .5VP. Oh, wait. You do want that.

> Or it could mean your prey had one pool when time ran out. There is
> an equal chance of either. Stop skewing the facts in your favor.

I'm not skewing the facts at all. I'm simply pointing out that position
when time runs out is just as likely to be losing as winning. So you
average the difference. .5VP.

> If you did, you get an extra vp for ousting. Why are you pretending I
> am trying to change that?

I'm not pretending anything. You spend an awful lot of time trying to
attribute motives to folks. That isn't really helping your argument.

> Are you trying to pretend my proposal does not reward him? It gives
> him 1 vp for ousting, plus one for last man standing, for a total of 2
> vp. It gives the same to a time-out player if AND ONLY IF he scores
> the same number of ousts. A time out player who scores no ousts gets
> only 1`vp under my proposal.

Under the current rules, a time out player who scores no ousts gets
.5VP. Which is reasonable, given that a time out position is just as
likely to be good as bad. So you split the difference. .5VP.

And if you *are* in a good position and want to get the 1VP for ousting
rather than the .5VP for timing out? Take a risk. Play faster. Try
harder to oust your prey. Which is why .5VP for time out is a good idea.
It provides incentive to do things like take risks and play faster.

> It does not seem logical to me, because you are guilty of double
> counting. You want to reward the the last man standing for scoring
> more ousts, but have forgotten that he has already been awarded for
> this, to the extent that he has done it.

I don't want to reward the last man standing for scoring more ousts. I
want to reward the last man standing for being in a good position when
the game comes to an actual end.

> It is an appropriate example. You want to cheat by comparing the last
> man standing with 1 oust to the time out player with no ousts, and
> argue that the last man standing with one oust is more deserving. Of
> course he is! And my proposal gives him more -- it gives him 1 extra
> vp for that extra oust that he got.

No, it is a ridiculous example because when is someone going to oust 3
people and then decide to withdraw? If it is 'cause they can't oust the
other last guy? Then the other last guy is in an advantageous position.
Give him the 1VP for being last man standing. Go him.

> You want to harp on the time out player with no ousts. But the
> appropriate comparison to the time out player with no ousts is the
> last man standing with no ousts.

I'm not harping on anything. I'm pointing out the being the last man
standing comes from being in an advantageous position (go you! 1VP!) and
being alive when the game times out is essentially a random position
(split the difference! .5VP!)

> If you want a less "ridiculous trumped up" example, we should compare
> the time out player with 3 ousts to the last man standing with 3
> ousts. To my mind, they are both equally deserving -- they have
> ousted three players, and should both get 4 vp.

Except that in one example, the game has come to a natural end and the
last man standing got there by virtue of being in a advantageous
position. And in the other, the game has come to an artificial,
essentially random end, and there is no way to know if either player is
in an advantageous position.

> You are assuming facts not in evidence. The only way E has foiled A
> is to avoid A's attempt to oust him. In other words, E survived until
> the end of the game. That is all E managed to accomplish -- not being
> ousted.

You can't be the last man standing without ousting someone or compelling
your opponent to withdraw. The only reason your opponent would withdraw
is 'cause you are in an advantageous position. If you are in a
disadvantageous position? Your opponent does not withdraw. Do you
actually play this game?

> I think you're getting a bit carried away. There is no reason to
> discuss collusion. If you prefer a different example, where A's
> motives might be clearer, how about 4 player game: A ousts B, then
> ousts C, then withdraws. E (wuss that he is) lets him. A wins 3 vp
> to 1 vp standard rules (2.5 vp to 1 vp VEKN rules).

Why does C withdraw? Unless E is in a strong position, C has zero reason
to withdraw. If E is in a strong position, he gets a reward for forcing
his opponent to withdraw.

> Here we see that

> A by withdrawing secures himself the game win. His motives are clear
> enough.

No, they aren't, 'cause people don't withdraw in situations like yo
describe. Withdrawl only comes from either lucky desperation or
negotiation. People in winning positions don't withdraw. The position
you are proposing as evidence for your argument is one of a player in a
winning position deciding to withdraw. Which doesn't happen. Unless they
are in a losing position. In which case the other player is forcing them
to withdraw. Which is as good as ousting them.

Messages.Author: LSJ

And AVG 42,17 != 1

Equally immaterial.

However, AVG of 0,2 does indeed = 1, which is the point.

If you'd like to extend to a 4p, AVG 0,0,0,4 = 1
This is not quite the point, though, since we aren't averaging all players'
accumulations (which is trivially 1, given the basic games' VP rules). We're
averaging the accumulations possible for one of the remaining players.

In With 2p left, player A can either oust B (2,0), get ousted (0,2) or have
either A or B withdraw (1,1). For A, these outcomes are 2,0, and 1. The average
of that set is 1. (The former 0,2 evaluation was omitting the withdrawal cases,
as it had previously mentioned it would be).

If you want to go properly to 4p, then you have to evaluate the possibilities
for player A at that point. That list, too, has a mean of 1 (this is also
relatively intuitive after noting the zero-sum aspect of the basic games' VP
rules, but requires a bit more analysis than the "average accumulation of all
players" stat).

Not make predictions, but analyze expected outcomes.

If A and B play a game where 10% of the time A wins a dollar and 90% of the time
B wins a dollar, then the expected outcome is 0.1 dollar for A. That is not the
same thing as predicting that A will win a dime (indeed, that outcome is not
possible).

If the game can be called on time (and no suitable way exists to analyze how far
from the expected norm the game state currently differs at any arbitrary point
in the game), then a natural thing to do would be to award A a dime (the
expected outcome; not the predicted outcome) when time is called.

> significant change.

True, the rules could be changed in any number of significant ways.
But that's not the issue yet. All this noise over the facts prevents any sort of
meaningful discussion toward that end.

The first step is understanding what is being said so that the decision on
change (if and how) could be approached.

To the extent that I understand your gist, you seem to be saying
something along the lines of the following: A player who (under the
standard rules zero-sum game paradigm) scores 1,1,1 in 3 preliminary
rounds (because he merely survived), should be ranked lower than a
player who, in the same three rounds, scores 0,0,3 (getting ousted in
the first two games, and winning in the last, because of his risk
taking strategies), even though both have scored, per the standard
rules, 3 total vps. You seem to be saying that the latter is more
deserving of making it to the finals. Am I correct?

If that is what you are saying, I agree 100%

I am in favor of preserving, intact, the vp system during tournament
play, for purposes of determining a game winner in accordance to the
standard rules, and/or time out rules in keeping with what I (however
arbitrarily) regard as in keeping with the standard rules. This does
not, however, mean that I want tournament ranking to be based solely
on vps. For me, the primary purpose of VPs is to be used for scoring
an individual game, particularly for determining a winner. Once they
have served that purpose, they can be dispensed with, and other
considerations may be used to determine tournament ranking.

First, imagine a tournament scoring system where VPs were the primary
means of tournament ranking, but that the standard rules were followed
with 1 full vp granted for time out, and no other consideration
trumped. Under this system the 1,1,1 player would do as well as the
0,0,3 player. This would be a Bad Thing! But I am not advocating
such a system!

Second, here come the DCI's rules. The DCI decides to solve this
problem by creating a half-point discount for survival in unfinished
games. Now the do-nothing, non-risk taking player gets .5,.5,.5, for
a total of 1.5, while the 0,0,3 player gets either 2.5 or 3 --
depending on whether his last game finished -- but in either case
beats the do-nothing player. This is an improvement, at least in
terms of the problem we are discussing. (My only objection would be
that the same result could have been achieved on a tournament level
without distorting the victory conditions on an in-game level).

Third, the VEKN introduces the Game Win system. Now the do-nothing
player still gets .5, .5, .5; and the risk taker still gets 0,0,2.5 or
0,0,3. However, now the risk taker gets something alot more valuable
thatn 1.5 extra vps. He gets a GAME WIN, which trumps any number of
VPs. Now the incentive to PLAY TO WIN becomes even stronger. (The in-
game victory conditions, however, remain distorted from the standard
rules -- unnecessarily in my view).

Fourth, here comes my initial proposal from my initial thread. Now the
do nothing player once again gets 1, 1, 1, for a total of 3; the risk
taker now gets 0,0,3. They are once again tied for VPs, but this
barely matters any more because the risk taker has a GAME WIN and the
do-nothing player has not. Because of this all important difference,
System Fourth no longer has the flaw of System First.

But still, this does not punish the do-nothing player quite as much as
the third proposal did, and it remains possible that this do-nothing
player might still make the finals in a very small tournament. Hence,
my Second proposal (System Fifth, below)

Fifth, here comes my second proposal. Now the do-nothing player gets .
2,.2,.2 (or other appropriate figure, for instance, if one prefers to
keep it at 0.5) for a total of 0.6, while the 0,0,3 player gets 3,
plus a GAME WIN. Now, even in a small tournament generating less
than 5 game winners, the 1,1,1 do nothing player will not only lose to
the 0,0,3 game winning risk taker, but will also lose to the moderate
0,1,2 risk taker who fails to score a game win (this guy gets
0,.2,1.5 -- for a total of 1.7). This is achieved without actually
distorting the victory conditions of the original game, because the
unmodified victory points are used only for in-game purposes, and the
modified victory points (or "victory score") is used for ranking
purposes.

You cannot, in fairness, accuse me of desiring to reward the do-
nothing player. Only for in-game purposes do I want him to get a full
vp, and for in-game purposes that full point is useless to him unless
he can get two more. In the standard game, the victory point is
merely an intermediate step to determining the identity of the winner,
and the relative ranking of the remaining players.

prey and survival. The theme of the game is to devour one's enemy and
try not to be devoured oneself -- eat or be eaten. There should be no
other methods of winning or losing. My proposal restores that
purity. A person may gain a victory point for withdrawing, but he
does not gain an advantage over his opponent (or over players at other
tables) by doing so -- he merely survives, and leaves his opponents
equally alive as he found them.

The current system does not have that purity. The worst abuses are
removed, but other potential opportunities remain. It is still
possible to gain an advantage by forcing one's opponent to withdraw
(which is neither eating nor being eaten).

Also, if, at the end of a deadlocked game, one player has an ancilla
empowerment in his hand, players can all cooperate to reduce their
pool to an appropriate level, and then vote for the ancilla
empowerment, simultaneously ousting everyone. Such a situation is not
a vicious "eat or be eaten" struggle, but an incestuous "lets all eat
each other" orgy. It ends in a 5-way tie, but with 1, 1, 1, 1, 1
instead of .5, .5, .5, .5, .5. It ends the game, but without any
player getting the better of anyone else. Such situations may be
rare, but they can occur, and they violate the spirit of the game.

My proposal avoids that. The only way to get an advantage is to oust
your enemy -- and not let your enemy oust you.

I doubt you'll find any. The DCI rules are old. I cannot remember a
time they were not in effect.

One function suggested was a "risk incentivization" device, and also
possibly intended to serve similar function to the game win system --
insure that a player who scored 0,0,3 in three preliminary rounds got
a higher tournament score than he who merely survived til time and got
what might otherwise have been 1,1,1. Nowadays, the former would be
ranked higher anyway, because he gets a GAME WIN in addition to his 3
vps. But under the DCI rules, the game win system was not yet in
effect, so the do-nothing survivor instead gets reduced to 0.5, 0.5,
0.5 (total 1.5) and is well behind the player with 0, 0, 3. Now we
have both the DCI discount and the Game Win system, and it is not
clear (to me) that we need both.

The DCI discount created a distortion, however, where one type of
deadlock was worth more than another. Players realized if they were
deadlocked by the clock, they could cooperate for mutual profit and
create another type of deadlock. Thus, they maximized their vps by
cooperation rather than by vicious competition -- totally in violation
of the spirit of the game. Nobody eats or gets eaten, but everyone
makes a profit. The VEKN put a stop to this by reducing the
withdrawal award to 0.5 -- making it once again the same as the
survival award. This eliminated the artificial withdrawal incentive
-- one however, that would never have been present in the first place
but for the half vp discount.

know some other guy's opinion. We can have our own opinions, and do
our own analysis, without access to his mind. Each system, and each
change, is laid out before us in black and white.

Evidently so. When I worked with the mentally retarded, there used to
be a policy of giving them little gold stars as rewards for good
behavior. Though retarded, they were still smart enough not to care.
They knew that the little gold stars, though pretty, were completely
useless. Occasionally, efforts were made to address this problem by
promising a meaningful reward if enough little gold stars could be
accumulated.

So please explain, why are you so afraid that people will get a WHOLE
victory point that they get for mere survival. What do you think they
are going to do with that victory point. Are you worried that they
will stick it on their hat, take it home, and proudly show it to
mommy? Or sell it on ebay? Or take it to the streat corner and buy a
dime bag of crack cocaine? What do you think they want it for?

In casual games, the only thing it is really good for is that, like
the little gold stars, if you collect enough of them, you can get
something you really want -- a GAME WIN. This is also their primary
function in tournaments -- though they also have a secondary function
as second tier tie breakers (though they don't have to be used this
way). A person who is satisifed to earn just one vp, earns nothing
for his trouble. He certainly is not going to get into the finals in
any tournament where more than 5 players score game wins.

This "reward" for survivability that you are so afraid of is as
illusory as the "reward" of the little gold stars. To achieve
anything worthwhile, you need more than one vp. You need to oust your
opponents. You need to get the better of your opponents, and merely
surviving does not help you do that.

Perhaps you have lost the context. The example under discussion --
one I chose -- refers to the player who has already scored two ousts,
and has 2 vp in the bank. There is one player left for him to
devour. If he ousts that last player he gains 1.5 vp (compared to
time out); if he gets ousted, he loses (compared to time out) 0.5 vp
AND A GAME WIN. Because the game win is worth 3,000,000 vps in this
context, it is impossible to bribe the player with vps. He is worried
about losing the game win.

My (second) system does not attempt to bribe THIS player to finish the
game. Instead, it bribes his opponent. His opponent either has 0 vp
or 1 vp, and therefore, under my second proposal, will have incentives
equal to (if he has 1 vp) or greater than (if he has 0 vp) those
offered by the current system. Hence I encourage him to take the
offensive. My system bribes the player who can be bribed.

So, my system incentivizes risk taking in all contexts, because there
is always a player with less than 2 vp who can be bribed. I bribe the
player with 0 vp, and I bribe the player with 1 vp. I do not try to
bribe the player with 2 vp, because I know that is impossible -- no vp
bribe will be outweigh what he has to lose.

I do not bother bribing the player with 3 vp, because I figure he is
doing well enough, and also because continued escalation of reward
will make 5-player tables too valuable compared to 4-player tables.
He already has a game win fer crissakes -- no matter what happens --
even if he gets ousted. A game that goes to time after a game winner
has already been firmly and irrevocably determined is not a priority
for me.

I really think I have all bases covered -- the 0 vp player gets
greater incentives than currently; the 1 vp player get incentives
equal to or greater than those that exist currently depending on
context(and which do not only come into play when there are 2 players
left); I have shown that incentivizing the 2 vp player is a lost
cause. That leaves only the player with 3 vps, who has already scored
a game win, regardless of whether he later gets ousted. Do you really
think the latter guy needs an incentive?

If you don't like my example, choose another one. Any example you
mention (with the possible exception of the 3 vp case), I can show
that my system offers the more effective incentives to ousting and
risk taking -- regardless of whether the next oust will result in last
man standing.

it mean the guy with 2 VP in the bank will always play conservatively
in preference to risking a little to get the extra 1.5 VP. It depends
on his perception of the risks of losing the game and rewards in the
tournament standings of 1.5 extra victory points. People with game
wins miss out on the finals for lack of 1.5 VP all the time. Hell,
it's not infrequent that tournament points (the tie-breaker after

player was a wash. He got 1.5 "table score" for two victory points

proposal, VPs in the current system), so it's the same either way.
All your second proposal does is _remove_ the 0.5 table score bribe
in this situation.

> So, my system incentivizes risk taking in all contexts, because there

> doing well enough, and also because continued escalation of reward
> will make 5-player tables too valuable compared to 4-player tables.

incentive with the threaten 0.5 VP dock. And the 0.5 VP is certainly
worth something. It is _not_ "useless".

> equal to or greater than those that exist currently depending on
> context(and which do not only come into play when there are 2 players
> left); I have shown that incentivizing the 2 vp player is a lost
> cause.

I don't agree you've shown any such thing. In fact, it's a
disincentive in my book. A guy with 1 VP who may or may not oust
someone near time stands to gain 1.5 table score if he does. In
the current rules, it's only worth 1.5 if it resolves the game. In
your second proposal, it's worth 1.5 whether or not it resolves the
game - thus, disincentive. But worse, a player who got 2 ousts and
got ousted actually *loses* 0.5 table score in your second proposal.
In my book, a guy who got ousted after gaining 2 VP has done a lot
to resolve a game and this change is a distinct disincentive to take
risks.

Well, certainly yes. I do. You know that.

I like your example just fine. It just doesn't show what you claim.

Fred

taking is to measure what the player stands to gain and to lose while
he still has an opportunity to act. By this standard my proposal
incentivises risk.

stands to lose 1.3 and stands to gain 1.5. This could be easily
changed by juggling the numbers. The reason I give a minimal
incentive at this stage is that the 1 vp player is withing striking
distance of a game win, and I figure this will so dominate his
motivations that vp incentives become irrelevant. Therefore, I find
it more productive to focus the vp incentives on the 0 vp player --
but this could be altered.

ouster deserves more than the do-nothing survivor is the case where 5
players are close to time out, and one player plays an ancilla
empowerment, ousting everyone simultaneously (perhaps everyone votes
in favor after reducing their pool per agreement). The result under
the current rules -- everyone gets 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 instead of .5, .5, .

nothing to get the better of their opponents -- they just arranged a
different kind of 5-way tie. It's just another variation of the old

game win will dominate motivations. The 3 vp player already has a
game win, and needs no incentives from anyone.

This puts the focus on the right place. The point in the game where
everyone has 0 vp is the point where the game is the slowest.
Eliminate half these players and the problem is almost solved, and the
game proceeds much more quickly thereafter.

Frederick Scott wrote:
> You can think surviving-to-timeout compares approximately to
> withdrawal if you want.

I do, and I have pointed out objectively verifiable similarites. The
standard rules follow the following formula: Each player starts with
1 vp gains 1 vp every time he ousts, and loses 1 vp if he gets
ousted. Period (no need to add anything for withdrawal or last man
standing). The formula does not have to be stated this way (and in
fact was not stated this way) but the end result always complies with
this simple formula.

To avoid subtracting of vps, the standard rules do not award the
"starting" 1 vp (the one the player brings to the table) until it is
determined that he will keep it -- that he will not be ousted. Hence,
he gains 1 vp when he withdraws, becausd that is when it is determined
he will not be ousted. Hence, when the game ends, any player still in
the jyhad(there can be only one per the standard rules) gets 1 vp.

The standard rules do not like even scores -- the players are supposed
to play until they eat or get eaten; deadlock is regrettable. Hence,
withdrawal is made almost impossible unless your prey decides to let
you. But when some kind of deadlock regrettably occurs, the
withdrawer gets 1 vp. This is not to "reward" him for withdrawing
(this is something the rules actively discourage by making withdrawal
virtually impossible) -- it simply to acknowledge the fact that he was
never ousted, and therefore is still owed the vp he would get under
the simple formula mentioned above.

Time-out is an equally regrettable deadlock -- a necessary evil.
Under the same philosophy, time outers should get 1 vp; not to
"reward" them, but simply to acknowledge the fact that they were never
ousted.

You can argue, as you do, that they should be treaded differently, to
incentivize risk. But I have certainly pointed out how they are
similar and it is silly to pretend I have not. It is simply a rude
refusal to acknowlege your opponent's position.

> But I don't and others you seem to be
> debating about it seem to share my skepticism.

> and demand. If you increase the supply while keeping the demand

> Economics of VTES 101

If you increase the supply of one metal, it will typically reduce the
value of that metal, but not of all metals. An increased supply of
gold will result in an reduced price for gold, but need hardly result
in a reduced price for copper, especially when you need the copper for
a purpose that gold will not serve.

Two ousts will still get you game win, and are generally needed as
well. You cannot get a game win merely by surviving. Those two
ousts, and the vps that come with them, are as scarce as ever.
